effect: Life-threatening colchicine toxicity: multiorgan failure, bone marrow suppression, neuromuscular paralysis.
mechanism: Clarithromycin potently inhibits both CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, raising colchicine AUC 7-10 fold.
action: Absolutely contraindicated. If macrolide needed, use azithromycin with extreme caution or a non-interacting antibiotic.
monitoring: CBC, renal function, CK, neurological status

effect: Massive simvastatin accumulation causing rhabdomyolysis — potentially fatal acute kidney injury.
mechanism: Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4, increasing simvastatin AUC up to 10-fold.
action: Do not co-prescribe. Switch to pravastatin or rosuvastatin. If already combined, withhold simvastatin for the antibiotic course.

effect: Severe, potentially fatal bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia) and mucositis.
mechanism: Additive antifolate toxicity; trimethoprim also reduces renal tubular secretion of methotrexate, raising plasma levels.
action: Avoid in all settings including low-dose weekly MTX. Use alternative antibiotics. If unavoidable, admit for monitoring with folinic acid rescue.
monitoring: CBC with differential, renal function, oral mucosa

effect: Life-threatening colchicine toxicity.
mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, greatly raising colchicine levels.
action: Avoid. Use doxycycline or amoxicillin instead.

effect: Serotonin syndrome: hyperthermia, clonus, agitation, autonomic instability — can be fatal.
mechanism: Linezolid is a non-selective reversible MAO-A inhibitor; escitalopram blocks serotonin reuptake causing massive serotonin accumulation.
action: Never combine. Stop SSRI at least 2 weeks before linezolid (5 weeks for fluoxetine). Consider cyproheptadine or ICU care if toxicity occurs.

effect: Rhabdomyolysis — severe muscle breakdown with acute kidney injury.
mechanism: Fluconazole is a potent CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 inhibitor, causing marked increase in simvastatin exposure.
action: Hold simvastatin for duration of fluconazole therapy. Switch to pravastatin or rosuvastatin if statin required.

effect: Serotonin syndrome: hyperthermia, neuromuscular excitability, autonomic instability.
mechanism: Dual serotonin excess: linezolid MAOI activity + fluoxetine/norfluoxetine (active metabolite, t½ 4-16 days) SSRI activity.
action: Contraindicated. Stop fluoxetine 5 weeks before linezolid due to long half-life of norfluoxetine.

effect: Fatal serotonin syndrome — hyperthermia, seizures, cardiovascular collapse.
mechanism: Catastrophic serotonin excess: MAOI prevents serotonin breakdown; fluoxetine blocks reuptake.
action: Never combine. 5-week washout after stopping fluoxetine before starting MAOI; 14-day washout after stopping MAOI before starting fluoxetine.

effect: Profound, potentially fatal hypotension — systolic BP can drop >80 mmHg.
mechanism: Both drugs increase nitric oxide/cGMP signalling causing additive vasodilation.
action: Absolutely contraindicated. No safe time window. Use alternative ED treatment (alprostadil) in patients requiring nitrates.

effect: Rhabdomyolysis risk — very high simvastatin plasma levels.
mechanism: Ketoconazole is the most potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; raises simvastatin AUC >10-fold.
action: Do not combine. Withhold simvastatin for duration of ketoconazole therapy.

effect: Serotonin syndrome.
mechanism: Linezolid MAO-A inhibition + sertraline SSRI activity.
action: Contraindicated. Discontinue sertraline at least 2 weeks before linezolid.

effect: Serotonin syndrome — severity varies by SSRI (worst with fluoxetine due to long half-life).
mechanism: Linezolid non-selective MAO inhibition + serotonin reuptake inhibition.
action: All SSRIs contraindicated with linezolid. Washout: fluoxetine 5 weeks; other SSRIs 14 days.

effect: Severe hypotension — potentially life-threatening.
mechanism: Both increase cGMP via nitric oxide pathway causing additive vasodilation.
action: Contraindicated. If emergency nitrate required after sildenafil, delay 24h; after tadalafil delay 48h. Treat hypotension with IV fluids and phenylephrine.

effect: Severe hypotension (tadalafil t-half 17.5h — risk window 48h).
mechanism: Additive nitric oxide/cGMP-mediated vasodilation.
action: Contraindicated. 48-hour tadalafil-free window required before nitrate administration.

effect: Severe, potentially fatal hyperkalaemia — cardiac arrest.
mechanism: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone-mediated potassium excretion; exogenous KCl adds to potassium load.
action: Do not co-prescribe routine KCl supplements with spironolactone. Monitor K+ closely if replacement unavoidable.

effect: Serotonin syndrome and/or seizures — can be fatal.
mechanism: Tramadol inhibits serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake; MAOIs prevent monoamine breakdown — massive neurotransmitter excess.
action: Absolutely contraindicated. 14-day washout after stopping MAOI before tramadol. Use morphine or fentanyl as alternative opioid.

effect: Profound hypotension, extreme sedation, bradycardia — potentially fatal.
mechanism: Ciprofloxacin potently inhibits CYP1A2, the primary metabolic pathway of tizanidine, increasing AUC 10-fold.
action: Absolutely contraindicated. Use alternative muscle relaxant (baclofen, diazepam) if ciprofloxacin needed.

effect: Hypertensive crisis and serotonin syndrome.
mechanism: Carbamazepine has structural similarity to tricyclic antidepressants; combination with MAOIs causes serotonin/norepinephrine excess.
action: Contraindicated. 14-day washout after stopping MAOI before starting carbamazepine.

effect: Potentially fatal QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 (raising domperidone levels) and both drugs independently prolong the QT interval.
action: Contraindicated. Use metoclopramide as alternative antiemetic. Obtain ECG if inadvertently co-administered.

effect: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Additive hERG channel blockade — both independently prolong QT interval.
action: Avoid combination. If antipsychotic needed during quinolone therapy, consider quetiapine with ECG monitoring.

effect: Risk of contrast-induced nephropathy leading to metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis.
mechanism: Contrast media can acutely impair renal function; metformin is renally cleared — accumulation causes inhibition of hepatic lactate metabolism.
action: Hold metformin 48h before and 48h after iodinated contrast. Check eGFR before restarting.

effect: Torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death.
mechanism: Additive IKr (hERG) blockade — both prolong the QT interval by independent mechanisms.
action: Avoid. Use amoxicillin or doxycycline as alternatives. If unavoidable, continuous cardiac monitoring required.

effect: Torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Additive QT prolongation — sotalol is a class III antiarrhythmic that blocks IKr; ciprofloxacin does the same.
action: Contraindicated. Use amoxicillin/clavulanate or alternative antibiotic.

effect: Complete loss of anticoagulant effect — INR collapses to sub-therapeutic within days, risking thromboembolism.
mechanism: Rifampicin is the most potent inducer of CYP2C9 (primary warfarin metabolic enzyme) known — warfarin AUC falls by 80-90%.
action: Avoid if possible. If TB treatment unavoidable, increase warfarin substantially (guided by daily INR). Reduce dose back on rifampicin completion.
monitoring: INR daily during initiation and dose titration

effect: Complete failure of gout treatment — pyrazinamide completely opposes allopurinol's effect.
mechanism: Pyrazinoic acid (pyrazinamide metabolite) inhibits renal tubular uric acid secretion, overwhelming allopurinol's xanthine oxidase inhibition.
action: Do not co-prescribe. Manage gout with colchicine during active TB treatment (avoid NSAIDs). Resume allopurinol after pyrazinamide phase.

effect: Severe CNS and respiratory depression — risk of coma and respiratory arrest.
mechanism: Additive potentiation at GABA-A receptors; both independently suppress CNS and respiratory drive.
action: Counsel all benzodiazepine patients strongly about alcohol avoidance. If combined use suspected, observe for 4-6h; consider flumazenil if severe.

effect: Severe CNS and respiratory depression.
mechanism: Synergistic GABA-A potentiation.
action: Avoid alcohol throughout benzodiazepine therapy. Counsel patient explicitly.

effect: Substantially increased risk of isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity. Daily alcohol raises risk of severe liver damage.
mechanism: Alcohol induces CYP2E1, converting isoniazid to hepatotoxic metabolites. Additive hepatocellular stress.
action: Strongly advise alcohol cessation during TB treatment. Monitor LFTs monthly. Stop isoniazid if ALT >3x ULN with symptoms or >5x ULN without.

effect: Lactic acidosis — particularly with binge drinking or fasting.
mechanism: Alcohol impairs hepatic gluconeogenesis and lactate clearance; metformin also inhibits mitochondrial respiratory chain Complex I.
action: Advise patients to avoid heavy or binge drinking. Regular moderate alcohol may be acceptable with normal renal function.
monitoring: Lactate (if symptomatic: nausea, abdominal pain, hyperventilation)

effect: Disulfiram-like reaction: severe flushing, headache, vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension.
mechanism: Metronidazole inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, causing toxic acetaldehyde accumulation.
action: Absolutely no alcohol during metronidazole therapy and for 48h after the last dose. Warn patient explicitly.

effect: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Additive hERG channel blockade. Amiodarone t-half approximately 40-55 days — interaction persists after amiodarone stopped.
action: Avoid. Use doxycycline or amoxicillin. If unavoidable, obtain ECG, correct electrolytes, monitor QTc.

effect: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Additive QT prolongation — ciprofloxacin blocks hERG channels; amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic.
action: Avoid. Use alternative antibiotic (amoxicillin/clavulanate, doxycycline). If unavoidable, ECG monitoring.

effect: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Additive hERG channel blockade.
action: Avoid. Use doxycycline or amoxicillin instead.

effect: QT prolongation and risk of torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4/CYP2C9 reducing amiodarone/desethylamiodarone clearance; both drugs prolong QT.
action: Avoid. Use alternative antifungal (terbinafine for dermatophytes; nystatin for Candida mucositis).

effect: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Additive hERG channel blockade.
action: Avoid. Use doxycycline or amoxicillin/clavulanate.

effect: Potentially fatal QT prolongation.
mechanism: Both block hERG (IKr) channels — additive QTc prolongation.
action: Avoid. Use metoclopramide or cyclizine as alternative antiemetics.

effect: Digoxin toxicity — nausea, bradycardia, AV block, arrhythmias.
mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4, raising digoxin levels by 70-100%. Plus additive AV node depression.
action: Reduce digoxin dose by 30-50% when starting amiodarone. Monitor digoxin levels and ECG. Target digoxin level 0.5-0.9 ng/mL.
monitoring: Digoxin level, ECG (PR interval, rhythm), HR

effect: Significantly raised INR — major bleeding risk.
mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits CYP2C9 (warfarin S-enantiomer). Effect persists weeks-months after amiodarone stopped.
action: Reduce warfarin dose by 30-50% when starting amiodarone. Monitor INR weekly until stable, then monthly. Effect persists for months after amiodarone stops.

effect: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp, raising simvastatin concentrations significantly.
action: Do not exceed simvastatin 20mg/day with amiodarone. Alternatively switch to pravastatin or rosuvastatin.

effect: Methotrexate toxicity — mucositis, myelosuppression.
mechanism: Penicillins compete with methotrexate for renal tubular secretion, raising MTX levels.
action: Avoid penicillins with methotrexate. If unavoidable (high-dose MTX), monitor closely and consider folinic acid.
monitoring: CBC, LFTs, renal function, mucous membranes

effect: Significantly increased bleeding risk — GI haemorrhage, intracranial bleeding.
mechanism: NSAIDs inhibit platelet aggregation and damage gastric mucosa; apixaban inhibits Factor Xa. Combined haemostatic impairment.
action: Avoid concomitant use. Use paracetamol for analgesia. If NSAID unavoidable, add PPI and use lowest dose for shortest duration.
monitoring: Signs of bleeding: haematemesis, melaena, haematuria

effect: Greatly increased bleeding risk — GI haemorrhage, major haemorrhage.
mechanism: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 (pharmacodynamic); at higher doses also displaces warfarin from protein binding.
action: Avoid unless dual indication exists (e.g., AF + recent ACS). Use lowest aspirin dose. Add PPI. Target INR lower end of range.

effect: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis — though less severe than with simvastatin.
mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, raising atorvastatin AUC approximately 4-fold.
action: Hold atorvastatin during clarithromycin therapy or switch to pravastatin/rosuvastatin.

effect: Myopathy risk.
mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4, raising atorvastatin levels.
action: Hold atorvastatin or switch to pravastatin during erythromycin course.

effect: Increased atorvastatin levels — myopathy risk.
mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP2C9, both involved in atorvastatin metabolism.
action: Reduce atorvastatin dose during fluconazole therapy or temporarily suspend.

effect: Marked reduction in atorvastatin efficacy — loss of lipid control.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, reducing atorvastatin AUC by approximately 80%.
action: Switch to rosuvastatin (least affected). Monitor LDL closely.

effect: QT prolongation — risk of torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Additive hERG channel blockade.
action: Avoid. Use metoclopramide as alternative.

effect: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Additive hERG channel blockade — both prolong QTc.
action: Avoid. Use alternative antibiotic (amoxicillin, doxycycline). ECG if co-administered.

effect: Markedly reduced levothyroxine absorption — hypothyroidism.
mechanism: Calcium carbonate forms poorly soluble complex with levothyroxine, preventing absorption.
action: Separate administration by at least 4 hours. Take levothyroxine fasting in the morning; calcium at lunchtime or evening.
monitoring: TSH (recheck 6-8 weeks after any change in timing)

effect: Carbamazepine toxicity — dizziness, diplopia, ataxia, nausea, confusion.
mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, the primary metabolic enzyme for carbamazepine, raising levels significantly.
action: Avoid. Use alternative antibiotic. If unavoidable, reduce carbamazepine dose and monitor level.

effect: Carbamazepine toxicity.
mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition raises carbamazepine levels.
action: Avoid. Use alternative antibiotic.

effect: Contraceptive failure — unintended pregnancy.
mechanism: Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4, accelerating oestrogen and progestogen metabolism.
action: Use copper IUD or depot injection. If OCP preferred, use preparation with at least 50mcg ethinylestradiol plus barrier method.
monitoring: Breakthrough bleeding (a sign of reduced efficacy)

effect: Reduced warfarin efficacy — sub-therapeutic INR, thromboembolic risk.
mechanism: Carbamazepine induces CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, increasing warfarin metabolism.
action: Monitor INR closely. Expect INR to fall within 1-2 weeks of starting carbamazepine. Significant dose increase may be needed.
monitoring: INR weekly for 4 weeks then monthly

effect: Up to 70% reduction in ciprofloxacin absorption — antibiotic failure.
mechanism: Iron chelates ciprofloxacin in the GI tract forming an insoluble complex.
action: Separate by at least 2 hours (ciprofloxacin before iron supplement).

effect: Theophylline toxicity — seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, nausea, vomiting.
mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, the main enzyme metabolising theophylline, raising levels by 20-80%.
action: Avoid. Use amoxicillin or doxycycline instead. If unavoidable, reduce theophylline dose by 30-50% and monitor level.

effect: Increased INR and bleeding risk.
mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2 (minor warfarin pathway) and reduces vitamin K-producing gut flora.
action: Monitor INR closely within 3-5 days of starting and stopping ciprofloxacin.

effect: Increased bleeding risk — GI haemorrhage.
mechanism: Additive platelet inhibition and gastric mucosal damage.
action: Avoid. Use paracetamol. Add PPI if any NSAID is necessary.

effect: Increased GI bleeding and potential reduction of clopidogrel antiplatelet effect.
mechanism: Ibuprofen may compete with clopidogrel for COX-1 binding; also causes GI mucosal damage.
action: Avoid. Use paracetamol. Add PPI if combination unavoidable.

effect: Severe hypoglycaemia.
mechanism: Trimethoprim inhibits renal tubular secretion of glibenclamide; sulphamethoxazole has intrinsic hypoglycaemic activity.
action: Avoid. Use alternative antibiotic. If unavoidable, monitor blood glucose 4-hourly and reduce glibenclamide dose.

effect: Severe hyperkalaemia — risk of cardiac arrest.
mechanism: ACEi reduces aldosterone; trimethoprim blocks distal tubule ENaC channels (potassium-sparing effect similar to amiloride).
action: Avoid combination in elderly and those with CKD. If unavoidable, check potassium within 5-7 days.

effect: Hyperkalaemia.
mechanism: ARB reduces aldosterone; trimethoprim blocks renal ENaC channels.
action: Monitor potassium within 5-7 days. Avoid in renal impairment.

effect: Life-threatening hyperkalaemia.
mechanism: Triple potassium-raising mechanism: spironolactone antagonises aldosterone + trimethoprim blocks ENaC channels.
action: Avoid combination especially in elderly or CKD. Closely monitor K+ if unavoidable.
monitoring: Serum potassium (daily if high risk), ECG

effect: Markedly elevated INR — major bleeding risk.
mechanism: Sulphamethoxazole inhibits CYP2C9 (warfarin S-enantiomer primary metabolism); also reduces gut flora.
action: Monitor INR within 2-3 days of starting co-trimoxazole. May need 25-50% warfarin dose reduction.

effect: Serotonin syndrome and dextromethorphan toxicity (hallucinations, confusion).
mechanism: Fluoxetine strongly inhibits CYP2D6 (dextromethorphan metabolism) and has serotonergic activity.
action: Avoid cough preparations containing dextromethorphan with fluoxetine. Use alternative antitussive.

effect: Methotrexate toxicity — mucositis, myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity.
mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin synthesis, decreasing renal blood flow and MTX clearance. Also compete for tubular secretion.
action: Avoid NSAIDs within 24-48h of weekly methotrexate dose. Use paracetamol for analgesia.

effect: Significantly increased bleeding risk — especially GI haemorrhage.
mechanism: Diclofenac inhibits platelet aggregation (pharmacodynamic) and inhibits CYP2C9 (pharmacokinetic), raising warfarin levels.
action: Avoid. Use paracetamol for pain. If NSAID unavoidable, add PPI and check INR within 3-5 days.

effect: Digoxin toxicity — nausea, bradycardia, AV block.
mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits P-glycoprotein, raising serum digoxin levels by 70-80%.
action: Reduce digoxin dose by 25-50% when starting clarithromycin. Monitor digoxin level and ECG.

effect: Elevated INR and major bleeding risk.
mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 (R-warfarin) and reduces gut flora.
action: Monitor INR within 2-3 days of starting clarithromycin.

effect: Digoxin toxicity — nausea, bradycardia, AV block, arrhythmias.
mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits P-glycoprotein and eliminates gut bacteria that inactivate digoxin.
action: Monitor digoxin levels within 5-7 days of starting erythromycin. Check ECG. Consider dose reduction.

effect: Digoxin toxicity plus additive AV nodal suppression — severe bradycardia, complete heart block.
mechanism: Verapamil inhibits P-glycoprotein (raises digoxin by 50-75%) and directly suppresses AV nodal conduction.
action: Reduce digoxin dose by 30-50% when starting verapamil. Monitor ECG, HR, digoxin level. Target level 0.5-0.9 ng/mL.
monitoring: Digoxin level, ECG (PR interval, rhythm), HR

effect: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
mechanism: Diltiazem inhibits CYP3A4, raising simvastatin AUC 3-5 fold.
action: Do not exceed simvastatin 10mg/day with diltiazem. Alternatively switch to pravastatin or rosuvastatin.

effect: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4, raising domperidone levels; both independently prolong QT.
action: Avoid. Use metoclopramide as antiemetic.

effect: Hyperkalaemia — cardiac arrhythmias.
mechanism: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone secretion, impairing renal potassium excretion; exogenous KCl raises potassium load.
action: Avoid routine KCl supplementation with ACEi. Monitor K+ closely if replacement required.

effect: Theophylline toxicity — seizures, arrhythmias, nausea.
mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits CYP1A2 and CYP3A4, reducing theophylline clearance by 25-50%.
action: Avoid. Use doxycycline or amoxicillin. If unavoidable, reduce theophylline dose and monitor level.

effect: Elevated INR and bleeding risk.
mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and reduces vitamin K-producing gut flora.
action: Monitor INR within 2-3 days of starting erythromycin.

effect: QT prolongation — risk of torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Additive hERG channel blockade; escitalopram prolongs QTc dose-dependently.
action: Avoid high-dose ondansetron (>16mg IV). Consider alternative antiemetic (metoclopramide, cyclizine).

effect: Up to 79% reduction in levofloxacin absorption — antibiotic failure.
mechanism: Iron chelates fluoroquinolone in GI tract.
action: Separate by at least 2 hours (levofloxacin first, then iron).

effect: Reduced levothyroxine absorption — hypothyroidism.
mechanism: Iron forms insoluble complex with levothyroxine in GI tract.
action: Separate by at least 4 hours. Take levothyroxine fasting; iron later in the day.

effect: Severe hypoglycaemia.
mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9, raising glibenclamide AUC approximately 2-fold.
action: Avoid. Consider switching to insulin temporarily. Monitor blood glucose 4-hourly if unavoidable.

effect: Severe hypoglycaemia.
mechanism: CYP2C9 inhibition by fluconazole raises gliclazide levels.
action: Avoid. Monitor glucose intensively if unavoidable.

effect: Severe hypoglycaemia.
mechanism: CYP2C9 inhibition raises glimepiride exposure.
action: Avoid. Monitor blood glucose intensively if unavoidable.

effect: Greatly reduced fluconazole efficacy — antifungal failure.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4, reducing fluconazole plasma levels by approximately 75%.
action: Avoid co-administration during active antifungal treatment. Consider liposomal amphotericin B if both TB and fungal infection require treatment.

effect: Markedly elevated INR — major bleeding risk.
mechanism: Fluconazole strongly inhibits CYP2C9 (warfarin S-enantiomer), raising plasma levels dramatically.
action: Reduce warfarin dose by 25-50%. Monitor INR every 2-3 days during fluconazole therapy.

effect: Serotonin syndrome and reduced tramadol analgesia.
mechanism: Fluoxetine inhibits CYP2D6 (blocks tramadol activation) and adds serotonin burden.
action: Avoid. Use morphine or oxycodone as alternative opioid analgesics.

effect: Increased INR and bleeding risk.
mechanism: Fluoxetine inhibits CYP2C9; SSRIs also have pharmacodynamic antiplatelet effects.
action: Monitor INR 1 week after starting/stopping fluoxetine.

effect: Rhabdomyolysis risk — simvastatin levels up to 3x higher.
mechanism: Grapefruit juice irreversibly inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 via furanocoumarins, increasing simvastatin bioavailability.
action: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice entirely with simvastatin therapy.

effect: Methotrexate toxicity — potentially fatal myelosuppression and mucositis.
mechanism: Ibuprofen reduces renal blood flow by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, impairing MTX clearance. Also competes for tubular secretion.
action: Avoid NSAIDs with methotrexate. Use paracetamol. If NSAID unavoidable, ensure adequate hydration and monitor CBC and renal function.

effect: Major bleeding — GI haemorrhage risk significantly increased.
mechanism: Additive impairment of haemostasis: NSAID inhibits platelets and damages gastric mucosa; rivaroxaban inhibits Factor Xa.
action: Avoid concomitant use. Use paracetamol. If NSAID unavoidable, add PPI and use shortest course.
monitoring: GI symptoms, haematological signs of bleeding

effect: Significantly increased bleeding risk.
mechanism: Ibuprofen inhibits platelet aggregation and erodes gastric mucosa; may also displace warfarin from albumin binding.
action: Avoid. Use paracetamol. If NSAID required, add PPI, use lowest effective dose, monitor INR.

effect: Phenytoin toxicity — nystagmus, ataxia, cognitive slowing.
mechanism: Isoniazid is a potent inhibitor of CYP2C9, the main enzyme metabolising phenytoin, raising levels significantly.
action: Monitor phenytoin levels closely when starting or stopping isoniazid. Dose reduction of phenytoin may be needed.

effect: Lamotrigine toxicity — rash (risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome), dizziness, diplopia, tremor.
mechanism: Valproate inhibits UGT1A4 (glucuronidation of lamotrigine), approximately doubling lamotrigine half-life.
action: Halve the usual starting dose of lamotrigine. Slow titration mandatory. Monitor for skin rash — stop immediately if rash develops.
monitoring: Skin examination, lamotrigine level, neurological symptoms

effect: Hyperkalaemia — potentially fatal.
mechanism: ACEi reduces aldosterone; spironolactone blocks aldosterone receptor. Additive potassium retention.
action: Avoid in CKD stage 3b+. If used (heart failure), check K+ and creatinine within 1 week of starting, then monthly.

effect: Hyperkalaemia.
mechanism: ARB + aldosterone antagonist — dual potassium-raising effect.
action: Monitor K+ closely. Avoid in CKD.

effect: Severe bradycardia and complete heart block — cardiac arrest risk.
mechanism: Pharmacodynamic synergy: both drugs depress SA node automaticity, AV node conduction, and myocardial contractility.
action: Avoid combination if possible. Never give IV verapamil to a patient on beta-blockers. If oral combination used, monitor ECG and HR continuously.

effect: Markedly elevated INR — bleeding risk.
mechanism: Metronidazole inhibits CYP2C9 and possibly CYP3A4, raising warfarin levels. Also reduces vitamin K-producing gut bacteria.
action: Reduce warfarin dose by 25-50%. Monitor INR within 2-3 days of starting and after stopping metronidazole.

effect: Increased bleeding risk.
mechanism: Naproxen inhibits platelet aggregation and can cause GI mucosal damage.
action: Avoid. Use paracetamol. Add PPI if NSAID is unavoidable.

effect: Contraceptive failure.
mechanism: Phenytoin induces CYP3A4, accelerating oestrogen and progestogen metabolism.
action: Use copper IUD or depot injection. If OCP preferred, use at least 50mcg ethinylestradiol plus barrier method.

effect: Hyperkalaemia.
mechanism: ACEi reduces aldosterone — impairs renal K+ excretion; KCl adds exogenous potassium.
action: Avoid routine KCl supplementation. Monitor K+ closely.

effect: Massive loss of simvastatin effect — total loss of lipid control.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, reducing simvastatin AUC by over 90%.
action: Switch to rosuvastatin (least affected by CYP3A4 induction).

effect: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
mechanism: Verapamil inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp, raising simvastatin AUC approximately 4-fold.
action: Do not exceed simvastatin 10mg/day with verapamil. Switch to pravastatin or rosuvastatin.

effect: Hyperkalaemia.
mechanism: ARB + aldosterone antagonist — dual potassium retention.
action: Monitor K+ closely, especially in CKD.

effect: Serotonin syndrome and reduced analgesia.
mechanism: SSRIs inhibit CYP2D6 (prevents tramadol activation) and add serotonergic activity.
action: Avoid tramadol in all patients on SSRIs. Use morphine or oxycodone as alternatives.

effect: Complete contraceptive failure.
mechanism: Rifampicin is the most potent CYP3A4 inducer, reducing oestrogen and progestogen levels by over 80%.
action: Use copper IUD during and for 28 days after rifampicin. Barrier method mandatory if OCP continues.

effect: Sub-therapeutic INR — thromboembolic events (stroke, DVT, PE).
mechanism: Rifampicin is the most potent CYP2C9 inducer, reducing warfarin S-enantiomer AUC by 80-90%.
action: Avoid if possible. If co-prescribed, increase warfarin substantially guided by daily INR. Reduce back to original dose 2 weeks after stopping rifampicin.
monitoring: INR daily during initiation then weekly

effect: Reduced metformin plasma levels — potentially inadequate glycaemic control.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces OCT1 and other organic cation transporters, increasing metformin renal clearance.
action: Monitor blood glucose closely during TB treatment. May need to increase metformin dose.

effect: Hypothyroidism — significantly reduced levothyroxine effect.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP enzymes involved in T4 metabolism, increasing thyroid hormone clearance.
action: Monitor TSH monthly during rifampicin therapy. Expect to need higher levothyroxine doses.

effect: Carbamazepine toxicity — ataxia, diplopia, confusion.
mechanism: Isoniazid inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP2C19, reducing carbamazepine metabolism.
action: Reduce carbamazepine dose. Monitor carbamazepine plasma level weekly during initiation of TB treatment.

effect: Valproate toxicity — sedation, confusion, thrombocytopenia.
mechanism: Isoniazid inhibits CYP2C9 and may impair valproate metabolism.
action: Monitor valproate levels and LFTs closely during INH therapy.

effect: Significantly reduced ethambutol absorption — risk of TB treatment failure.
mechanism: Aluminium hydroxide adsorbs ethambutol in the GI tract, reducing peak plasma concentration by approximately 50%.
action: Separate by at least 4 hours (ethambutol first, then antacid).

effect: Complex interaction — INR may rise initially then fall below therapeutic range.
mechanism: Biphasic: phenytoin initially inhibits CYP2C9 (raises warfarin), then induces CYP2C9 (lowers warfarin). Warfarin may also raise phenytoin levels.
action: Monitor INR and phenytoin levels closely. Interaction is unpredictable — requires frequent monitoring.

effect: Significantly elevated INR — major bleeding risk.
mechanism: Metronidazole inhibits CYP2C9 and reduces vitamin K-producing gut bacteria.
action: Monitor INR within 2-3 days of starting metronidazole. Warfarin dose reduction often needed.

effect: Elevated INR and bleeding risk.
mechanism: Sertraline mildly inhibits CYP2C9; all SSRIs independently inhibit platelet aggregation.
action: Monitor INR 1 week after starting sertraline. Add PPI if patient at GI bleeding risk.

effect: Digoxin toxicity — bradycardia, AV block, arrhythmias.
mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits P-gp and CYP3A4, raising digoxin levels by 70-100%.
action: Reduce digoxin dose by 50% when starting amiodarone. Monitor digoxin level and ECG.

effect: Up to 80% reduction in quinolone absorption — antibiotic failure.
mechanism: Divalent and trivalent cations (Al3+, Mg2+, Ca2+) in antacids chelate quinolones in the GI tract.
action: Separate by at least 2 hours (quinolone first, then antacid — or antacid 6h before quinolone).

effect: Methotrexate toxicity.
mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal MTX clearance and compete for tubular secretion.
action: Avoid NSAIDs with methotrexate. Use paracetamol.

effect: Lithium toxicity — tremor, confusion, cardiac arrhythmia, renal failure.
mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin synthesis, decreasing renal blood flow and lithium clearance — lithium levels rise 25-60%.
action: Avoid NSAIDs in patients on lithium. Use paracetamol. If NSAID unavoidable, reduce lithium dose and monitor level within 3-5 days.
monitoring: Lithium plasma level (target 0.6-1.0 mmol/L), renal function, neurological symptoms

effect: Lithium toxicity.
mechanism: Diclofenac reduces renal prostaglandin synthesis, impairing lithium clearance.
action: Avoid all NSAIDs with lithium. Use paracetamol.

effect: Lithium toxicity — ACEi impair renal lithium excretion.
mechanism: ACEi reduce glomerular filtration pressure and cause compensatory sodium retention in the proximal tubule, which also retains lithium.
action: Monitor lithium level within 1 week of starting ACEi, and every 3 months thereafter. May need 25-50% lithium dose reduction.

effect: Lithium toxicity — potentially severe.
mechanism: Thiazide diuretics cause sodium depletion; the kidney compensates by reabsorbing more sodium (and lithium) in the proximal tubule, raising lithium levels by 25-40%.
action: Reduce lithium dose by 25-40% when starting thiazide. Monitor level closely.
monitoring: Lithium level every 3-5 days until stable

effect: Increased apixaban exposure — major bleeding risk.
mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits both CYP3A4 and P-gp, the two elimination pathways of apixaban, raising AUC approximately 1.6-fold.
action: Avoid co-administration. Use alternative antibiotic (amoxicillin, doxycycline).

effect: Increased rivaroxaban exposure — bleeding risk.
mechanism: CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibition by clarithromycin raises rivaroxaban AUC.
action: Avoid if possible. Use amoxicillin or doxycycline instead.

effect: Major bleeding risk — rivaroxaban levels rise significantly.
mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp — both major rivaroxaban elimination pathways.
action: Avoid. Use alternative antifungal (nystatin locally for Candida).

effect: Reduced haloperidol efficacy — loss of antipsychotic control.
mechanism: Carbamazepine potently induces CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, reducing haloperidol plasma levels by 50-60%.
action: May need to double haloperidol dose. Monitor for relapse of psychotic symptoms.

effect: Reduced valproate levels plus carbamazepine-epoxide (toxic metabolite) accumulation.
mechanism: Carbamazepine induces valproate metabolism; valproate inhibits carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide (toxic metabolite) conversion to the diol.
action: Monitor both drug levels. Check carbamazepine-epoxide level if toxicity suspected.
monitoring: Valproate level, carbamazepine level plus epoxide

effect: Complex: valproate initially raises phenytoin free fraction (displaces from albumin), then total level may fall.
mechanism: Valproate displaces phenytoin from protein binding and inhibits CYP2C9.
action: Monitor free (unbound) phenytoin level rather than total. Interpret total level with caution.

effect: Risk of acute kidney injury leading to metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis.
mechanism: High-dose furosemide reduces renal function (pre-renal azotaemia), impairing metformin clearance.
action: Monitor renal function when initiating or increasing furosemide. Hold metformin if creatinine rises acutely.

effect: Hypoglycaemia — more frequent and severe than with other fluoroquinolones.
mechanism: Ciprofloxacin blocks pancreatic K-ATP channels, stimulating insulin secretion.
action: Monitor blood glucose 4-hourly during ciprofloxacin therapy. Use alternative antibiotic if possible.

effect: Acute kidney injury (triple whammy: ACEi + NSAID + dehydration).
mechanism: NSAIDs block prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriole dilation; ACEi reduce efferent constriction — glomerular filtration pressure collapses.
action: Avoid NSAID + ACEi combination, especially with concurrent diuretic. Use paracetamol.

effect: Acute kidney injury and attenuated antihypertensive effect.
mechanism: NSAID + ACEi — loss of dual renal autoregulatory mechanisms.
action: Avoid. Use paracetamol. Check renal function if NSAID essential.

effect: Acute kidney injury and antihypertensive attenuation.
mechanism: NSAID + ACEi combination — collapse of glomerular filtration.
action: Avoid. Monitor renal function within 1 week if unavoidable.

effect: Acute kidney injury and reduced antihypertensive efficacy.
mechanism: ARB + NSAID — dual impairment of renal autoregulation.
action: Avoid. Use paracetamol.

effect: Acute kidney injury and antihypertensive attenuation.
mechanism: ARB + NSAID.
action: Avoid. Use paracetamol.

effect: Acute kidney injury and reduced antihypertensive effect.
mechanism: ARB + NSAID.
action: Avoid. Use paracetamol.

effect: Methotrexate toxicity — PPIs raise MTX levels by impairing renal elimination.
mechanism: PPIs inhibit renal tubular BCRP/MRP2 transporters that secrete MTX, reducing clearance by 20-50%.
action: Hold PPI 24h before and restart 24h after high-dose MTX infusion. For low-dose weekly MTX, monitor more frequently if PPI needed.
monitoring: MTX level, CBC, renal function, mucositis

effect: Very high risk of GI ulceration and haemorrhage.
mechanism: Corticosteroids deplete mucosal prostaglandins; NSAIDs also inhibit COX — synergistic gastrotoxicity.
action: Avoid. If both required, add PPI (omeprazole 20mg) and use shortest NSAID course. Prefer paracetamol.
monitoring: GI symptoms, haemoglobin, stool for occult blood

effect: GI ulceration and haemorrhage.
mechanism: Additive gastrotoxicity — corticosteroid + NSAID.
action: Avoid combination. Use paracetamol. Add PPI if NSAID unavoidable.

effect: Unpredictable INR changes — usually increased anticoagulation.
mechanism: Corticosteroids may inhibit warfarin hepatic metabolism; complex pharmacokinetic interaction.
action: Monitor INR within 1 week of starting or stopping prednisolone, especially at high doses.

effect: Digoxin toxicity secondary to hypokalaemia.
mechanism: Thiazides cause renal potassium loss; hypokalaemia sensitises the myocardium to digoxin toxicity.
action: Monitor K+ closely. Replace K+ if below 3.5 mmol/L. Target K+ 3.5-5.0 mmol/L.

effect: Digoxin toxicity secondary to hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia.
mechanism: Loop diuretics cause renal loss of K+ and Mg2+; both electrolyte deficiencies sensitise the heart to digoxin.
action: Replace potassium and magnesium as needed. Monitor electrolytes monthly.

effect: Bradycardia and hypotension — metoprolol toxicity.
mechanism: Fluoxetine potently inhibits CYP2D6, the main enzyme metabolising metoprolol, raising metoprolol AUC 4-fold.
action: Reduce metoprolol dose or switch to bisoprolol or atenolol (not CYP2D6 substrates).

effect: Reduced doxycycline efficacy — potential antibiotic failure.
mechanism: Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4, accelerating doxycycline metabolism and halving its half-life.
action: Use alternative antibiotic not affected by CYP3A4 induction (amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav).

effect: Reduced doxycycline plasma levels — antibiotic failure.
mechanism: Phenytoin induces CYP3A4, reducing doxycycline half-life significantly.
action: Use amoxicillin or alternative non-CYP3A4 substrate antibiotic.

effect: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Additive hERG channel blockade.
action: Avoid combining two QT-prolonging antiemetics. Use one agent at lowest effective dose.

effect: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Additive hERG blockade.
action: Avoid combining two dopamine antagonists with QT effects.

effect: Elevated INR when hypothyroidism corrected — bleeding risk.
mechanism: Hyperthyroid state increases catabolism of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X; correcting hypothyroidism raises anticoagulant sensitivity.
action: Monitor INR closely when initiating or adjusting levothyroxine. Warfarin dose reduction usually needed as euthyroid state is achieved.
monitoring: INR every 2-4 weeks during levothyroxine dose titration

effect: Ibuprofen may antagonise the antiplatelet effect of low-dose aspirin.
mechanism: Ibuprofen reversibly blocks the COX-1 active site, preventing aspirin's irreversible acetylation of the serine residue needed for permanent platelet inhibition.
action: If both needed, take aspirin at least 30 minutes before ibuprofen (or 8+ hours after) to ensure aspirin's irreversible binding occurs first.

effect: Elevated INR — dose-dependent. Risk is with regular use at doses above 2g/day.
mechanism: Paracetamol metabolites (NAPQI) inhibit the VKOR enzyme involved in vitamin K recycling; also mild CYP2C9 inhibition at higher doses.
action: Safe to use paracetamol at or below 2g/day with warfarin. Avoid prolonged use above 2g/day. Monitor INR if regular paracetamol is added or stopped.
monitoring: INR at 1 week if starting regular paracetamol use

effect: Increased risk of hepatotoxicity — combination raises risk significantly above either drug alone.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP2E1, increasing production of the hepatotoxic isoniazid metabolite (acetylhydrazine). Combined liver injury risk is additive to synergistic.
action: Monitor LFTs at baseline and monthly. Stop both if ALT above 3x ULN with symptoms or above 5x ULN without symptoms. Restart sequentially when levels normalise.
monitoring: LFTs monthly (ALT, AST, bilirubin), symptoms of hepatitis

effect: Significantly reduced doxycycline levels — antibiotic failure.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 and potentially other metabolic enzymes, reducing doxycycline half-life.
action: Avoid combination. If treating Brucellosis, use rifampicin plus co-trimoxazole instead.

effect: Increased risk of skin rash — usually maculopapular, occasionally severe.
mechanism: Not fully understood; possibly immune-mediated. Risk is approximately 3x higher than either drug alone.
action: Warn patient about rash. If rash occurs, determine which drug is responsible before stopping both.

effect: Symptomatic hypotension — dizziness, syncope especially on standing.
mechanism: Additive vasodilation — both alpha-blockers and PDE5 inhibitors lower vascular resistance.
action: Avoid initiation within 4 hours of an alpha-blocker dose. Start PDE5 inhibitor at lowest dose. Tamsulosin is safest alpha-blocker with sildenafil.
monitoring: BP sitting and standing, symptoms of hypotension

effect: Raised atorvastatin levels — myopathy risk.
mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp.
action: Do not exceed atorvastatin 40mg/day with amiodarone. Monitor CK.

effect: Hypotension — increased amlodipine levels.
mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, reducing amlodipine clearance.
action: Monitor BP during clarithromycin therapy. Consider reducing amlodipine dose.
monitoring: BP, signs of amlodipine excess (flushing, oedema)

effect: Increased simvastatin levels — myopathy risk.
mechanism: Amlodipine mildly inhibits CYP3A4, raising simvastatin AUC approximately 1.6-fold.
action: Do not exceed simvastatin 20mg/day with amlodipine. Consider rosuvastatin for higher statin doses.

effect: Elevated INR — modest increase.
mechanism: Antibiotic reduces vitamin K-producing intestinal flora.
action: Monitor INR within 3-5 days of starting and after stopping.

effect: Significantly reduced ciprofloxacin absorption — antibiotic failure.
mechanism: Chelation of ciprofloxacin by divalent/trivalent cations in antacids.
action: Separate by at least 2 hours. Take ciprofloxacin 2h before or 6h after antacid.

effect: Reduced doxycycline absorption by 40-50%.
mechanism: Chelation by divalent/trivalent cations.
action: Separate by 2-3 hours.

effect: Reduced levothyroxine absorption — hypothyroidism.
mechanism: Antacids bind levothyroxine in the GI tract.
action: Separate by at least 4 hours. Take levothyroxine fasting in the morning.

effect: Increased atorvastatin levels — myopathy risk (less than simvastatin).
mechanism: Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4, increasing atorvastatin bioavailability.
action: Advise patients to avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice with atorvastatin therapy.

effect: Reduced ciprofloxacin absorption.
mechanism: Calcium chelates ciprofloxacin.
action: Separate by at least 2 hours.

effect: Reduced doxycycline absorption.
mechanism: Calcium chelates doxycycline.
action: Separate by 2-3 hours.

effect: Carbamazepine toxicity — dizziness, drowsiness, ataxia.
mechanism: Isoniazid inhibits CYP3A4 reducing carbamazepine metabolism.
action: Monitor carbamazepine level and neurological status.

effect: Risk of acute kidney injury leading to metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis.
mechanism: NSAID reduces renal perfusion; metformin is entirely renally cleared.
action: Avoid regular NSAID use with metformin, especially in elderly or those with CKD.

effect: Reduced lamotrigine efficacy — seizure risk.
mechanism: Oestrogen induces UGT1A4, increasing lamotrigine glucuronidation and reducing its plasma level by approximately 50%.
action: Increase lamotrigine dose when starting OCP. Monitor seizure frequency. Pill-free week causes lamotrigine level to surge — watch for toxicity.

effect: Hyperkalaemia.
mechanism: ACEi impairs aldosterone-mediated potassium excretion.
action: Avoid potassium supplements unless documented hypokalaemia. Monitor K+.

effect: Hyperkalaemia.
mechanism: ARB reduces aldosterone.
action: Monitor K+ closely if supplement required.

effect: Reduced paracetamol analgesia and increased hepatotoxicity risk with prolonged use.
mechanism: Phenytoin induces CYP2E1 and CYP3A4, shunting more paracetamol through the hepatotoxic NAPQI pathway.
action: Use lowest effective paracetamol dose. Avoid prolonged use. Do not exceed 2g/day.

effect: Reduced clopidogrel antiplatelet effect by 40-50%.
mechanism: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, preventing conversion of clopidogrel prodrug to its active thiol metabolite.
action: Switch to pantoprazole (weakest CYP2C19 inhibitor) if PPI is needed alongside clopidogrel. Avoid omeprazole and esomeprazole.

effect: Reduced codeine analgesia AND risk of codeine toxicity in ultra-rapid metabolisers.
mechanism: Fluoxetine inhibits CYP2D6, blocking codeine conversion to morphine (the active analgesic).
action: Avoid codeine with fluoxetine. Use non-opioid analgesia or switch to morphine or oxycodone.

effect: Metoprolol accumulation — bradycardia and hypotension.
mechanism: Fluoxetine potently inhibits CYP2D6, the primary metabolic enzyme for metoprolol.
action: Reduce metoprolol dose or switch to bisoprolol or atenolol.

effect: High risk of GI ulceration and haemorrhage.
mechanism: Corticosteroids deplete mucosal prostaglandins; NSAIDs inhibit COX — synergistic gastrotoxicity.
action: Avoid. Add PPI if both required. Prefer paracetamol.

effect: Unpredictable INR changes — usually increased anticoagulation.
mechanism: Corticosteroids may inhibit warfarin hepatic metabolism.
action: Monitor INR within 1 week of starting or stopping prednisolone at high doses.

effect: Risk of acute kidney injury leading to metformin accumulation.
mechanism: High-dose furosemide reduces renal function, impairing metformin clearance.
action: Monitor renal function when initiating or increasing furosemide. Hold metformin if creatinine rises.

effect: Increased diazepam levels — excessive sedation.
mechanism: Isoniazid inhibits CYP2C19 and CYP3A4, reducing diazepam metabolism.
action: Monitor for excessive sedation. Consider dose reduction.

effect: Significantly reduced metoprolol efficacy — loss of BP and HR control.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP2D6, reducing plasma metoprolol levels by over 80%.
action: Increase metoprolol dose guided by HR and BP. Switch to bisoprolol or atenolol.

effect: Loss of antihypertensive effect.
mechanism: Rifampicin potently induces CYP3A4, reducing amlodipine AUC by approximately 90%.
action: Switch to antihypertensive less affected by CYP3A4 induction. Consider ACEi (not affected).

effect: Raised methotrexate levels — toxicity risk.
mechanism: PPI inhibits BCRP transporter in renal proximal tubules, reducing methotrexate secretion.
action: Hold PPI around high-dose MTX. For low-dose weekly MTX, monitor more closely.

effect: QT prolongation.
mechanism: Both prolong QT; erythromycin also inhibits CYP3A4, raising domperidone levels.
action: Avoid combining. Use alternative antiemetic.

effect: Modest elevation of INR.
mechanism: Doxycycline reduces vitamin K-producing gut bacteria.
action: Monitor INR within 5-7 days of starting doxycycline.

effect: Reduced lamotrigine levels — possible seizure breakthrough.
mechanism: Carbamazepine induces UGT enzymes, increasing lamotrigine glucuronidation.
action: Increase lamotrigine dose by 50-100% when used with carbamazepine. Monitor lamotrigine level.

effect: Reduced doxycycline absorption by up to 80%.
mechanism: Iron chelates doxycycline in GI tract.
action: Separate by at least 3 hours (doxycycline first).

effect: Moderately elevated metoprolol levels — mild bradycardia possible.
mechanism: Sertraline is a moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor, raising metoprolol levels.
action: Monitor HR and BP. Consider switching to bisoprolol or atenolol if bradycardia occurs.

effect: Worsening glycaemic control.
mechanism: Corticosteroids cause insulin resistance and raise blood glucose.
action: Monitor blood glucose closely when starting or stopping corticosteroids.

effect: Reduced doxycycline efficacy.
mechanism: Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4, accelerating doxycycline metabolism.
action: Use amoxicillin or co-amoxiclav instead.

effect: Minor reduction in azithromycin peak concentration (not clinically significant for most infections).
mechanism: Mild chelation by antacid cations.
action: Separate by 1-2 hours if clinically concerned, but not usually necessary.

effect: Mildly elevated metoprolol levels.
mechanism: Sertraline is a moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor.
action: Monitor HR and BP. Usually clinically insignificant but switch to bisoprolol if bradycardia occurs.

effect: Increased hepatotoxicity risk in chronic heavy drinkers — not in moderate drinkers.
mechanism: Chronic alcohol induces CYP2E1, shunting paracetamol to hepatotoxic NAPQI pathway.
action: Limit paracetamol to at or below 2g/day in heavy drinkers. Avoid in established alcoholic liver disease.
monitoring: LFTs if prolonged combined use in heavy drinker

effect: Mildly reduced levothyroxine absorption.
mechanism: PPI raises gastric pH; levothyroxine dissolution is pH-dependent.
action: Monitor TSH annually. Take levothyroxine at least 30-60 minutes before omeprazole.

effect: Enhanced hypoglycaemia and disulfiram-like reaction with some sulphonylureas.
mechanism: Alcohol potentiates sulphonylurea-induced insulin secretion and may inhibit gluconeogenesis.
action: Advise patients to avoid alcohol or drink minimally with sulphonylureas.

effect: Modestly reduced ciprofloxacin absorption.
mechanism: PPI raises gastric pH, slightly reducing ciprofloxacin dissolution.
action: No routine action needed for most infections. Separate by 2h for serious infections if possible.

effect: Amiodarone increases phenytoin levels by 2-3 fold, causing toxicity (ataxia, nystagmus, mental changes).
mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits CYP2C9, the main enzyme metabolising phenytoin.
action: Monitor phenytoin levels within 1-2 weeks of starting amiodarone. Reduce phenytoin dose by 30-50%.
monitoring: Phenytoin levels, cerebellar signs (ataxia, nystagmus, diplopia)
alternative: Levetiracetam (not CYP2C9-dependent) as alternative antiepileptic

effect: Spironolactone can interfere with digoxin immunoassay, causing falsely elevated or reduced levels, and may reduce digoxin renal clearance.
mechanism: Spironolactone and its metabolite canrenone cross-react with digoxin immunoassay. Also reduces renal tubular secretion.
action: Be aware of assay interference when interpreting digoxin levels in patients on spironolactone. Use specific digoxin assay if available. Monitor clinically for toxicity.
monitoring: Digoxin clinical toxicity signs rather than relying on assay; ECG
alternative: None required — awareness and clinical monitoring

effect: Amlodipine increases tacrolimus levels moderately, requiring dose monitoring.
mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition by amlodipine reduces tacrolimus clearance.
action: Monitor tacrolimus trough levels closely when amlodipine is started or stopped. Dose adjust as needed.
monitoring: Tacrolimus trough levels within 5-7 days of amlodipine change
alternative: No switch needed; monitoring and dose adjustment sufficient

effect: Loop diuretics markedly potentiate aminoglycoside ototoxicity — risk of permanent hearing loss.
mechanism: Both are independently ototoxic; furosemide causes cochlear oedema that concentrates aminoglycosides in the inner ear.
action: Avoid concurrent use if possible. If essential, use lowest effective aminoglycoside dose with once-daily dosing, monitor renal function and audiometry.
monitoring: Audiometry, tinnitus, hearing changes; renal function
alternative: Alternative antibiotic class (carbapenems, cephalosporins) if clinically appropriate

effect: Combination greatly increases risk of permanent sensorineural hearing loss and nephrotoxicity.
mechanism: Additive ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; furosemide concentrates gentamicin in cochlear fluid.
action: Avoid if possible. If used together, monitor renal function daily, check gentamicin levels, and assess hearing regularly.
monitoring: Renal function, gentamicin levels (trough <1 mg/L), audiometry if prolonged course
alternative: Consider carbapenem or extended-spectrum cephalosporin

effect: ACEi + aldosterone antagonist causes dangerous hyperkalaemia — potentially fatal cardiac arrest.
mechanism: Both reduce aldosterone activity — additive potassium retention in the kidney.
action: Indicated in heart failure (HFrEF) under strict monitoring: K+ and creatinine within 1 week, monthly for 3 months, then every 3 months. Stop if K+ >5.5 mmol/L or creatinine rise >30%.
monitoring: Serum K+ and creatinine at 1 week, monthly x3, then 3-monthly
alternative: If K+ >5.5, reduce/stop spironolactone; do not stop ACEi first

effect: Can cause fatal bradycardia, complete heart block, and cardiac arrest — particularly dangerous with IV verapamil.
mechanism: Additive AV node depression from beta-blockade and calcium channel blockade.
action: Never combine any beta-blocker with IV verapamil. Oral combination requires extreme caution and ECG monitoring only in hospital.
monitoring: Heart rate, ECG — PR interval, AV block
alternative: Use amlodipine instead of verapamil/diltiazem if rate control needed with beta-blocker

effect: Dual antiplatelet therapy increases bleeding risk. GI bleeding risk is approximately doubled vs monotherapy.
mechanism: Additive platelet inhibition via different mechanisms — COX-1 (aspirin) + P2Y12 (clopidogrel).
action: Use only when guideline-indicated (post-ACS, post-PCI). Always co-prescribe a PPI (pantoprazole preferred). Limit to guideline-defined duration.
monitoring: GI bleeding signs (melaena, haematemesis), haematuria, skin bruising
alternative: Restrict to evidence-based indications; add PPI; review regularly for bleeding risk

effect: Amiodarone moderately increases apixaban exposure by inhibiting P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4.
mechanism: Amiodarone and desethylamiodarone inhibit P-gp and CYP3A4, two key pathways for apixaban elimination.
action: No dose adjustment routinely required, but be aware of increased bleeding risk. Consider lower apixaban dose in patients with other bleeding risk factors.
alternative: Warfarin with close INR monitoring

effect: Amiodarone modestly increases rivaroxaban levels.
mechanism: P-glycoprotein inhibition by amiodarone increases rivaroxaban absorption and reduces elimination.
action: Monitor for increased bleeding risk. No dose reduction usually required unless other risk factors present.
alternative: Warfarin with INR monitoring as alternative

effect: Diltiazem increases atorvastatin levels approximately 2-3 fold, increasing myopathy risk.
mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition by diltiazem.
action: Limit atorvastatin to 40mg/day with diltiazem. Monitor for muscle symptoms.
alternative: Rosuvastatin or pravastatin (less CYP3A4-dependent)

effect: Linezolid's MAO-inhibiting properties combined with tramadol's serotonergic effect can cause serotonin syndrome.
mechanism: Additive serotonergic activity — linezolid inhibits MAO (raising synaptic serotonin) while tramadol blocks serotonin reuptake.
action: Avoid combination. Use morphine or oxycodone for analgesia in patients on linezolid.
monitoring: Serotonin syndrome: hyperthermia, clonus, agitation, tachycardia
alternative: Morphine or oxycodone (no serotonergic activity)

effect: Combination causes pseudotumour cerebri (benign intracranial hypertension) — severe headache, visual disturbance, papilloedema.
mechanism: Both independently cause raised intracranial pressure through unknown mechanisms; combined effect is dramatic.
action: Never co-prescribe. Use alternative acne antibiotic (erythromycin topical) or delay antibiotic until after isotretinoin course.
monitoring: Headache, visual disturbance, papilloedema if combination inadvertently given
alternative: Topical clindamycin or topical erythromycin for acne during isotretinoin

effect: Ciprofloxacin can both increase and decrease phenytoin levels unpredictably — either toxicity or seizure breakthrough possible.
mechanism: Complex interaction: CYP1A2 inhibition may raise levels; ciprofloxacin also reduces phenytoin absorption.
action: Monitor phenytoin levels closely during ciprofloxacin therapy. Watch for toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia) and also for breakthrough seizures.
alternative: Non-quinolone antibiotic where possible in epileptic patients

effect: Levofloxacin can potentiate warfarin and raise INR, though the effect is variable between patients.
mechanism: CYP1A2 inhibition and gut flora disruption (reducing vitamin K production).
action: Monitor INR within 3-5 days of starting levofloxacin in warfarin-treated patients.
alternative: Amoxicillin-clavulanate where appropriate (less INR effect)

effect: Rifampicin markedly reduces verapamil plasma levels, causing loss of antiarrhythmic and antihypertensive effect.
mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 induction dramatically increases verapamil first-pass metabolism.
action: Avoid combination or increase verapamil dose substantially with close monitoring. When rifampicin is stopped, reduce verapamil dose immediately to prevent toxicity.
alternative: Amlodipine (less affected by rifampicin though still somewhat reduced)

effect: Furosemide can increase lithium levels causing toxicity through sodium and fluid depletion.
mechanism: Volume depletion from loop diuretics triggers compensatory proximal tubular sodium (and lithium) retention.
action: Monitor lithium levels within 5 days of starting furosemide. Ensure adequate hydration and sodium intake. Reduce lithium dose if levels rise.
alternative: Amlodipine preferred for hypertension in lithium patients; avoid diuretics where possible

effect: Combination rarely causes severe neurotoxicity — encephalopathy, extrapyramidal signs, irreversible brain damage — even at normal lithium levels.
mechanism: Uncertain; haloperidol may increase lithium entry into neurons.
action: Use with extreme caution if combination is unavoidable. Monitor lithium levels closely. At first sign of neurotoxicity, stop both drugs immediately.
monitoring: Lithium levels, neurological status — confusion, extrapyramidal signs, fever
alternative: Atypical antipsychotics (e.g. quetiapine, olanzapine) have less severe interaction with lithium

effect: Combination causes serotonin syndrome; tramadol also lowers seizure threshold in SSRI-treated patients.
mechanism: Tramadol inhibits serotonin reuptake and weakly inhibits MAO; combined with SSRI causes serotonin excess.
action: Avoid. Use paracetamol or ibuprofen for analgesia in SSRI-treated patients. If opioid needed, use morphine (minimal serotonergic effect).
monitoring: Temperature, pulse, clonus, agitation, GI symptoms
alternative: Paracetamol or ibuprofen; morphine for severe pain

effect: Aspirin displaces valproate from plasma protein and inhibits its metabolism, causing valproate toxicity (tremor, sedation, encephalopathy).
mechanism: Aspirin displaces valproate from albumin (raises free fraction) and inhibits beta-oxidation of valproate.
action: Avoid high-dose aspirin with valproate. If low-dose aspirin (75-100mg) required, monitor valproate levels and clinical response.
monitoring: Valproate levels (especially free fraction), tremor, sedation, encephalopathy
alternative: Low-dose aspirin (75mg) is generally tolerated; avoid anti-inflammatory doses

effect: Additive CNS depression — excessive sedation, respiratory depression, coma.
mechanism: Both enhance GABA-A receptor activity, causing additive CNS depression.
action: Counsel strongly to avoid alcohol during benzodiazepine treatment.
alternative: Non-pharmacological anxiety management; if alcohol dependence present, address this first

effect: Fluconazole raises quetiapine levels significantly, increasing QT prolongation and CNS adverse effects.
mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition by fluconazole increases quetiapine exposure.
action: Reduce quetiapine dose or use alternative antifungal (e.g., topical). Monitor for QT prolongation and sedation.
alternative: Topical antifungal where clinically appropriate; or use caspofungin

effect: Ciprofloxacin inhibits quetiapine metabolism, raising levels and increasing QT prolongation risk.
mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition plus additive QT prolongation.
action: Use shorter quetiapine dose if combination unavoidable. Monitor ECG.
alternative: Non-fluoroquinolone antibiotic where clinically appropriate

effect: Mutual induction — each drug accelerates the other's metabolism, reducing levels. May cause breakthrough seizures.
mechanism: Both are potent CYP inducers; combined induction increases clearance of both.
action: Monitor levels of both drugs after starting, stopping, or changing the dose of either. Seizure frequency monitoring is essential.
monitoring: Phenytoin and carbamazepine levels; seizure diary
alternative: Monotherapy with levetiracetam or lamotrigine preferred

effect: IV contrast can cause acute kidney injury; if metformin continues, lactate clearance is impaired causing lactic acidosis.
mechanism: Contrast nephropathy → reduced GFR → metformin accumulation → mitochondrial dysfunction → lactic acidosis.
action: Withhold metformin on the day of contrast and for 48 hours after. Recheck eGFR before restarting. No need to stop if eGFR stable >45 and low-osmolality contrast used.
monitoring: Serum creatinine and eGFR before and 48h after contrast
alternative: Procedural metformin management — no drug substitute needed

effect: Rifampicin reduces prednisolone levels by up to 60%, causing loss of anti-inflammatory effect or risk of adrenal crisis in patients on replacement doses.
mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 induction by rifampicin.
action: Double prednisolone dose when rifampicin is added. Monitor clinical response. Reduce back to baseline when rifampicin is stopped.
monitoring: Clinical inflammatory response; signs of adrenal insufficiency if on physiological replacement doses
alternative: No drug switch — dose adjustment is the management strategy

effect: Alcohol causes hypoglycaemia in insulin-treated patients by inhibiting gluconeogenesis and masking warning symptoms.
mechanism: Alcohol inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis; reduces cortisol and adrenaline hypoglycaemic counter-response.
action: Counsel insulin patients strictly: eat when drinking, never drink on an empty stomach, check blood glucose before sleep after alcohol. Wear medical alert ID.
monitoring: Blood glucose before sleep; CGM if available
alternative: Strict dietary counselling; alcohol avoidance preferred

effect: Itraconazole increases dexamethasone exposure significantly, causing iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome and HPA axis suppression.
mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 inhibition by itraconazole increases dexamethasone AUC 3-fold.
action: Reduce dexamethasone dose substantially when used with itraconazole. Monitor for Cushingoid features and HPA suppression.
monitoring: Cushingoid features, blood glucose, blood pressure
alternative: Caspofungin if antifungal therapy required in patients on dexamethasone

effect: Itraconazole increases apixaban exposure approximately 2-fold, greatly increasing bleeding risk.
mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition by itraconazole.
action: Avoid combination. Use caspofungin or topical antifungal instead. If unavoidable, halve apixaban dose and monitor closely.
alternative: Caspofungin for systemic fungal infections; topical for minor infections

effect: Ketoconazole increases rivaroxaban exposure 2.6-fold, causing serious uncontrolled bleeding risk.
mechanism: Potent dual inhibition of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein by ketoconazole.
action: Contraindicated — never combine. Use alternative antifungal.
monitoring: Avoid; if inadvertently co-administered, monitor for bleeding
alternative: Caspofungin or topical antifungal

effect: Carbamazepine reduces apixaban exposure by approximately 50%, causing anticoagulation failure.
mechanism: CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein induction by carbamazepine increases apixaban clearance.
action: Avoid combination. Consider warfarin (also affected but manageable with INR monitoring) under haematology guidance.
monitoring: Anti-Xa activity if available; thromboembolism signs
alternative: Warfarin with close INR monitoring; or lamotrigine/levetiracetam as antiepileptic alternative

effect: Additive bleeding risk — particularly at higher aspirin doses. GI and surgical bleeding risk increased.
mechanism: Heparin inhibits coagulation cascade; aspirin inhibits platelet function and damages GI mucosa.
action: Low-dose aspirin (75-100mg) with prophylactic heparin is generally acceptable perioperatively. Avoid high-dose aspirin with therapeutic heparin.
monitoring: Bleeding signs, haemoglobin, PTT if therapeutic heparin
alternative: Add PPI for GI protection; use lowest effective aspirin dose

effect: Ketoconazole dramatically increases cyclosporine levels 3-4 fold, causing nephrotoxicity and other toxicity.
mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition by ketoconazole.
action: Avoid combination. Reduce cyclosporine dose by 50-80% if ketoconazole unavoidable — requires daily level monitoring.
monitoring: Cyclosporine trough levels daily, serum creatinine, BP
alternative: Topical antifungal where possible; caspofungin for systemic infections

effect: Erythromycin significantly increases tacrolimus levels, causing nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.
mechanism: CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition by erythromycin.
action: Use azithromycin instead of erythromycin where possible. If erythromycin is necessary, monitor tacrolimus levels within 24-48 hours.
monitoring: Tacrolimus trough levels, creatinine, neurological status
alternative: Azithromycin (weaker inhibitor) or doxycycline

effect: Causes life-threatening bone marrow suppression — pancytopenia and fatal outcomes have been reported.
mechanism: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that inactivates 6-mercaptopurine (active metabolite of azathioprine).
action: Absolutely contraindicated. If allopurinol is needed in a patient on azathioprine, switch azathioprine to mycophenolate. If both must be used, reduce azathioprine to 25% of dose with weekly FBC.
monitoring: Weekly FBC — stop both immediately if neutropenia or thrombocytopenia
alternative: Mycophenolate mofetil instead of azathioprine; febuxostat instead of allopurinol

effect: Antacids (especially magnesium and aluminium hydroxide) reduce mycophenolate absorption by 17-37%.
mechanism: Chelation of mycophenolate mofetil by divalent/trivalent cations in the gut.
action: Separate mycophenolate from antacid administration by at least 2 hours.
monitoring: Clinical response — monitor for signs of rejection or reduced immunosuppression
alternative: Separate timing; use PPI instead of antacid if acid suppression needed

effect: Rifampicin reduces mycophenolic acid (active form) exposure by approximately 30-70%.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces UGT enzymes and P-glycoprotein, increasing mycophenolate clearance.
action: Avoid combination in transplant patients. If rifampicin is essential for TB, consult transplant team — dose adjustment and very close monitoring of graft function required.
monitoring: MPA levels (if available), creatinine, graft function
alternative: Rifabutin (weaker inducer) if TB treatment absolutely required

effect: Gabapentin significantly increases the respiratory depression and sedation risk of morphine and other opioids. Risk of death increased.
mechanism: Additive CNS depression; gabapentin potentiates opioid-induced respiratory depression through distinct mechanisms.
action: Use the lowest effective doses of both. Avoid in patients at high respiratory risk (COPD, sleep apnoea). Titrate slowly. Have naloxone available.
monitoring: Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, sedation level
alternative: Non-opioid analgesia; if combination necessary, lowest possible doses

effect: Tramadol lowers seizure threshold; valproate may partially protect, but breakthrough seizures can occur — and tramadol toxicity may cause seizures at lower doses in epileptic patients.
mechanism: Tramadol weakly inhibits seizure threshold; interaction with anticonvulsants is complex.
action: Avoid tramadol in all epileptic patients. Use alternative analgesic.
alternative: Paracetamol, ibuprofen, or low-dose morphine for pain

effect: Sertraline (moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor) reduces conversion of codeine to morphine, impairing analgesia.
mechanism: CYP2D6 inhibition reduces codeine activation. Effect less severe than fluoxetine but clinically significant.
action: Use morphine or oxycodone as alternative analgesia in patients on sertraline.
alternative: Morphine or oxycodone

effect: Fluconazole modestly increases theophylline levels by CYP1A2 inhibition.
mechanism: CYP1A2 inhibition reduces theophylline clearance.
action: Monitor theophylline levels and clinical toxicity during fluconazole therapy.
alternative: No switch needed — monitoring and dose adjustment sufficient

effect: Rifampicin reduces theophylline levels substantially, risking therapeutic failure (loss of bronchodilation).
mechanism: CYP1A2 induction by rifampicin increases theophylline clearance.
action: Increase theophylline dose when rifampicin is started; reduce back when stopped. Monitor levels closely.
monitoring: Theophylline levels, symptoms of asthma/COPD control
alternative: Consider alternative bronchodilator not metabolised by CYP1A2

effect: Carbamazepine reduces theophylline levels by inducing its metabolism.
mechanism: CYP1A2 induction by carbamazepine increases theophylline clearance.
action: Monitor theophylline levels when carbamazepine is started or stopped. Dose adjust accordingly.
alternative: Adjust theophylline dose; consider alternative bronchodilator

effect: Additive dopamine antagonism causes severe extrapyramidal reactions — akathisia, dystonia, tardive dyskinesia.
mechanism: Both block dopamine D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway.
action: Avoid combination. Use alternative antiemetic (ondansetron alone, cyclizine) in patients on antipsychotics.
alternative: Ondansetron (alone, not with QT-prolonging drugs) or cyclizine

effect: Omeprazole modestly increases valproate levels through reduced hepatic metabolism.
mechanism: CYP2C19 inhibition by omeprazole modestly reduces valproate metabolism.
action: Generally not clinically significant. Monitor for increased valproate adverse effects (tremor, weight gain) if omeprazole dose is high.
alternative: Pantoprazole (less CYP2C19 inhibition) as alternative PPI

effect: Combination causes significant hypotension — orthostatic dizziness and falls, particularly in elderly men.
mechanism: Alpha-1 blocker (tamsulosin) + PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil) both lower blood pressure through different mechanisms.
action: If both are clinically needed, start sildenafil at 25mg and monitor blood pressure. Counsel patient about orthostatic precautions. Avoid in patients with known cardiovascular disease.
monitoring: Blood pressure (lying and standing), dizziness, syncope
alternative: If ED treatment needed in BPH patient, use lowest sildenafil dose with BP monitoring

effect: NSAIDs reduce the antihypertensive and diuretic effect of thiazides, potentially precipitating hypertensive crisis or fluid overload.
mechanism: NSAIDs promote sodium retention via prostaglandin inhibition, opposing the diuretic mechanism.
action: Avoid regular NSAID use in hypertensive patients on thiazides. Use paracetamol for analgesia.
alternative: Paracetamol for analgesia

effect: NSAIDs reduce diuretic effect of furosemide (diuretic resistance) and worsen renal function in heart failure patients.
mechanism: Prostaglandin inhibition reduces renal blood flow and blocks furosemide's action at the loop of Henle.
action: Avoid regular NSAIDs in patients on furosemide for heart failure or fluid overload. Use paracetamol.
monitoring: Fluid balance, weight, renal function, BP
alternative: Paracetamol; topical NSAID if musculoskeletal pain

effect: High-dose fish oil (>3g/day) may potentiate warfarin anticoagulation modestly.
mechanism: Omega-3 fatty acids have mild antiplatelet and anti-thromboxane effects; may also inhibit CYP2C9.
action: Monitor INR if patient takes high-dose fish oil with warfarin. Standard dietary fish intake is generally safe.
alternative: Counsel to stick to dietary fish intake rather than supplements

effect: High-dose garlic supplements have antiplatelet effects and may potentiate warfarin.
mechanism: Allicin inhibits platelet aggregation; possible CYP2C9 inhibition at high doses.
action: Counsel warfarin patients to avoid garlic supplements (dietary garlic is safe). Monitor INR.
alternative: Dietary garlic is acceptable; avoid supplements

effect: High-dose ginger may modestly enhance warfarin effect through antiplatelet activity.
mechanism: Gingerols inhibit platelet thromboxane synthesis.
action: Dietary ginger is safe. Advise avoiding high-dose ginger supplements in warfarin-treated patients.
alternative: Dietary ginger (cooking quantities) is acceptable

effect: High-dose turmeric/curcumin supplements may inhibit platelet aggregation and potentiate warfarin.
mechanism: Curcumin inhibits COX and thromboxane; possible CYP2C9 inhibition at high doses.
action: Cooking quantities of turmeric are safe. Warn warfarin patients to avoid curcumin/turmeric supplements. Monitor INR.
alternative: Cooking quantities are acceptable

effect: Fenugreek may enhance anticoagulant effect of warfarin — case reports of INR elevation.
mechanism: Coumarin derivatives in fenugreek seeds may have anticoagulant properties.
action: Advise warfarin patients to avoid fenugreek supplements. Monitor INR.
alternative: Avoid supplement; dietary amounts in cooking are likely safe

effect: Vitamin K antagonises warfarin entirely — even small dietary changes in vitamin K intake cause INR fluctuations.
mechanism: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase; exogenous vitamin K bypasses this block.
action: Counsel patients to maintain consistent vitamin K intake in diet (consistent greens intake — not zero, but consistent). Avoid vitamin K supplements unless reversing warfarin intentionally.
monitoring: INR closely if diet changes; after large vitamin K intake
alternative: DOACs (less affected by dietary vitamin K)

effect: Profound hypotension — case reports of loss of consciousness.
mechanism: Both affect cardiovascular dopamine and serotonin receptors; combination causes unpredictable severe BP drop.
action: Contraindicated. Use alternative antiemetic (metoclopramide, domperidone) with apomorphine.
monitoring: Blood pressure if combination inadvertently given
alternative: Domperidone (specifically used with apomorphine in PD), metoclopramide

effect: Probenecid markedly increases methotrexate levels by reducing renal tubular secretion — severe toxicity risk.
mechanism: Probenecid inhibits OAT3 transporter, dramatically reducing methotrexate renal clearance.
action: Avoid combination. If probenecid needed for gout, consider alternative gout therapy (colchicine) during methotrexate treatment.
monitoring: Methotrexate levels, FBC, renal function, mucositis
alternative: Colchicine for gout in methotrexate patients (with caution — own interactions to consider)

effect: Dexamethasone reduces cyclosporine levels by CYP3A4 induction; cyclosporine may also raise dexamethasone levels.
mechanism: Bidirectional interaction via CYP3A4 — induction by dexamethasone and inhibition by cyclosporine.
action: Monitor cyclosporine trough levels when dexamethasone is started or stopped at high doses.
alternative: Prednisolone (often used with cyclosporine in transplant — well-characterised interaction)

effect: Topiramate (at doses >200mg/day) reduces OCP efficacy, risking contraceptive failure.
mechanism: CYP3A4 induction at higher doses increases ethinylestradiol metabolism.
action: Use alternative or additional contraception. Copper IUD preferred. If OCP is used, consider higher-dose formulation.
monitoring: Breakthrough bleeding as indicator of reduced hormone levels
alternative: Copper IUD; levonorgestrel IUD

effect: Valproate causes major congenital malformations (neural tube defects, cardiac defects, craniofacial abnormalities) and neurodevelopmental disorders in children exposed in utero.
mechanism: Inhibition of histone deacetylase disrupts embryonic gene expression during neural tube closure.
action: Absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy unless no alternative exists for epilepsy control. All women of childbearing age on valproate must use highly effective contraception. If pregnancy occurs, do NOT stop suddenly — seek urgent specialist review.
monitoring: Pregnancy test before initiation; regular pregnancy status in women of childbearing age
alternative: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam are preferred in women of childbearing potential

effect: Cyclosporine markedly increases colchicine levels, causing severe colchicine toxicity — myopathy, neurotoxicity, multi-organ failure.
mechanism: CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition by cyclosporine causes massive colchicine accumulation.
action: Contraindicated in patients with renal impairment on cyclosporine. If colchicine is needed, use smallest possible dose (maximum 0.5mg) and monitor closely for toxicity.
monitoring: GI toxicity, muscle weakness, neuropathy, FBC (pancytopenia)
alternative: Prednisolone or NSAIDs for acute gout in transplant patients

effect: Life-threatening bone marrow suppression — same mechanism as azathioprine interaction.
mechanism: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which inactivates 6-mercaptopurine, causing toxic accumulation.
action: Contraindicated. If allopurinol is needed, reduce mercaptopurine to 25% dose with weekly FBC monitoring.
alternative: Febuxostat instead of allopurinol; discuss with oncology team

effect: Combination can cause additive hypotension and increased peripheral oedema.
mechanism: Both agents cause vasodilation through different mechanisms — additive blood pressure lowering.
action: Counsel patient about positional dizziness. Use lowest effective sildenafil dose. Monitor blood pressure.
alternative: No switch required — lowest effective sildenafil dose with BP monitoring

effect: PDE5 inhibitors combined with alpha-blockers can cause profound hypotension — syncope and falls.
mechanism: Additive vasodilation from both agents — PDE5 inhibition and alpha-1 blockade both reduce systemic vascular resistance.
action: Use lowest tadalafil dose (5mg for daily use). Start PDE5 inhibitor at least 6 hours after alpha-blocker if same-day use. Avoid tamsulosin combination — tamsulosin 0.4mg causes least hypotension.
alternative: Tamsulosin has least hypotensive interaction among alpha-blockers

effect: Additive nephrotoxicity and hypokalaemia — potentially life-threatening electrolyte abnormalities.
