mechanism: Both are nephrotoxic and promote renal potassium wasting; combined effect dramatically worsens both.
action: Avoid if possible. If both required, monitor renal function daily, replace potassium and magnesium aggressively, and use the minimum necessary doses.
monitoring: Daily creatinine, eGFR, serum K+ and Mg2+
alternative: Liposomal amphotericin (less nephrotoxic); avoid loop diuretics if possible

effect: Carbamazepine markedly reduces ketoconazole levels, causing antifungal failure. Ketoconazole also raises carbamazepine levels.
mechanism: Bidirectional: carbamazepine (CYP3A4 inducer) reduces ketoconazole; ketoconazole (CYP3A4 inhibitor) raises carbamazepine.
action: Avoid combination. Use fluconazole with monitoring, or itraconazole solution. Monitor carbamazepine levels.
monitoring: Antifungal response; carbamazepine levels and toxicity signs
alternative: Fluconazole (with INR monitoring) or caspofungin

effect: Voriconazole increases sirolimus levels by ~11-fold, causing severe sirolimus toxicity.
mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 inhibition dramatically reduces sirolimus clearance.
action: Contraindicated. Use caspofungin as antifungal in patients on sirolimus.
monitoring: Sirolimus levels daily if inadvertently co-administered
alternative: Caspofungin

effect: Rifampicin reduces voriconazole levels by over 90%, making antifungal therapy completely ineffective.
mechanism: Potent CYP2C19, CYP3A4, and CYP2C9 induction by rifampicin.
action: Contraindicated. Use alternative antifungal (caspofungin, liposomal amphotericin B) or alternative TB regimen.
monitoring: Voriconazole levels (if available); clinical antifungal response
alternative: Caspofungin or liposomal amphotericin B

effect: Carbamazepine reduces voriconazole levels by ~98% — complete antifungal failure.
mechanism: Potent CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 induction.
action: Contraindicated. Switch antiepileptic to levetiracetam or valproate if voriconazole is needed.
alternative: Caspofungin; or switch carbamazepine to levetiracetam

effect: Phenytoin reduces voriconazole levels by ~70% and voriconazole raises phenytoin levels 2-fold.
mechanism: CYP2C9 inhibition by voriconazole raises phenytoin; CYP2C19 induction by phenytoin reduces voriconazole.
action: Double voriconazole maintenance dose when given with phenytoin. Reduce phenytoin dose and monitor levels.
monitoring: Voriconazole trough levels; phenytoin levels; clinical toxicity of both
alternative: Levetiracetam as alternative antiepileptic

effect: Itraconazole increases cyclosporine levels 2-3 fold, causing nephrotoxicity and other toxicity.
mechanism: CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition.
action: Reduce cyclosporine dose by 50% when starting itraconazole. Monitor levels daily initially.
monitoring: Cyclosporine trough levels, renal function, BP
alternative: Caspofungin (no significant CYP3A4 interaction)

effect: Itraconazole markedly potentiates warfarin — INR can triple.
mechanism: CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibition reduces warfarin metabolism.
action: Monitor INR every 2-3 days during itraconazole therapy. Reduce warfarin dose empirically.
alternative: Topical antifungal where possible

effect: Itraconazole increases digoxin levels by ~50%, causing toxicity.
mechanism: P-glycoprotein inhibition reduces digoxin renal tubular secretion.
action: Reduce digoxin dose and monitor levels closely when itraconazole is started.
alternative: Azole-free antifungal (caspofungin) where possible

effect: Fluconazole inhibits clopidogrel activation, reducing antiplatelet effect and increasing cardiovascular event risk.
mechanism: CYP2C19 inhibition blocks conversion of clopidogrel prodrug to active form.
action: Avoid combination. Use topical antifungal where possible. If systemic antifungal required, use caspofungin or voriconazole (less CYP2C19 inhibition for short courses).
monitoring: Platelet function if available; cardiovascular events
alternative: Topical antifungal; or use caspofungin

effect: Ritonavir increases simvastatin AUC by ~3000-fold — virtually certain rhabdomyolysis.
mechanism: Extremely potent CYP3A4 inhibition by ritonavir.
action: Absolutely contraindicated. Never use simvastatin or lovastatin with any ritonavir-containing regimen.
monitoring: CK, muscle symptoms if inadvertently given
alternative: Rosuvastatin (least affected) or pravastatin

effect: Rifampicin reduces ritonavir levels by 75%, causing complete antiretroviral failure.
mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 induction by rifampicin overwhelms ritonavir's CYP3A4 inhibition.
action: Never combine. In HIV-TB co-infection, use rifabutin (600mg 3x/week) instead of rifampicin with lopinavir/ritonavir. Consult ID specialist.
alternative: Rifabutin + dose-adjusted lopinavir/ritonavir; consult HIV specialist

effect: Ritonavir increases midazolam levels by up to 34-fold — profound sedation and respiratory depression.
mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 inhibition dramatically reduces midazolam clearance.
action: Oral midazolam is absolutely contraindicated with ritonavir. IV midazolam may be used with extreme caution and dose reduction in ICU settings only.
monitoring: Sedation level, respiratory rate if IV midazolam used
alternative: Lorazepam or oxazepam (not CYP3A4-dependent)

effect: Efavirenz reduces methadone levels by 50-60%, precipitating opioid withdrawal in stable patients.
mechanism: CYP3A4 and CYP2B6 induction by efavirenz accelerates methadone metabolism.
action: Increase methadone dose by 50-100% when starting efavirenz. Monitor for withdrawal signs closely.
monitoring: Withdrawal symptoms, methadone levels if available
alternative: Consider nevirapine (less methadone induction) or integrase inhibitor-based regimen

effect: NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow, increasing tenofovir nephrotoxicity risk.
mechanism: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilation, reducing GFR and tenofovir clearance.
action: Avoid regular NSAIDs in HIV patients on tenofovir. Use paracetamol for analgesia. Monitor renal function.
monitoring: eGFR, urine protein, phosphate (Fanconi syndrome marker)
alternative: Paracetamol for analgesia

effect: Aluminium-containing antacids reduce isoniazid absorption by up to 33%.
mechanism: Aluminium forms insoluble complex with isoniazid in the gut.
action: Separate isoniazid from antacid by at least 1 hour. Take isoniazid on an empty stomach.
alternative: Take isoniazid 1 hour before antacid

effect: Rifampicin reduces lopinavir levels by 75%, causing complete antiretroviral failure.
mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 induction by rifampicin.
action: Contraindicated. Use rifabutin instead of rifampicin in HIV/TB co-infection with lopinavir/ritonavir.
alternative: Rifabutin 150mg daily with lopinavir/ritonavir; consult HIV specialist

effect: Rifampicin reduces digoxin levels by 30-50%, potentially causing loss of rate control or antiarrhythmic effect.
mechanism: P-glycoprotein induction increases intestinal digoxin efflux and renal tubular secretion.
action: Monitor heart rate and digoxin levels. Increase digoxin dose as needed during rifampicin therapy. Reduce dose when rifampicin is stopped.
alternative: Rate control with beta-blocker (less affected by rifampicin) if possible

effect: Rifampicin reduces itraconazole levels to near zero — complete antifungal failure.
mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 induction makes itraconazole essentially non-bioavailable.
action: Contraindicated. Use caspofungin or liposomal amphotericin B instead.
alternative: Caspofungin or liposomal amphotericin B

effect: Efavirenz reduces artemether and lumefantrine levels significantly, risking malaria treatment failure.
mechanism: CYP3A4 induction by efavirenz increases metabolism of both antimalarial components.
action: Use artesunate-based regimens without lumefantrine where possible in HIV patients on efavirenz. Consult ID specialist.
alternative: Artesunate + amodiaquine (less affected); consult specialist

effect: Both prolong QT interval; combination significantly increases torsades de pointes risk.
mechanism: Additive hERG potassium channel blockade.
action: Avoid combination. If malaria prophylaxis needed with amiodarone, use doxycycline or atovaquone/proguanil.
alternative: Doxycycline or atovaquone/proguanil for malaria prophylaxis

effect: Chloroquine modestly increases digoxin levels, increasing toxicity risk.
mechanism: Possible P-glycoprotein inhibition and reduced renal digoxin clearance.
action: Monitor digoxin levels and ECG during chloroquine course.
alternative: No switch needed — monitoring sufficient for short chloroquine courses

effect: Quinine doubles digoxin levels, causing digoxin toxicity.
mechanism: P-glycoprotein inhibition by quinine reduces digoxin renal clearance.
action: Reduce digoxin dose by 50% during quinine therapy. Monitor levels.
monitoring: Digoxin levels, ECG, bradycardia, nausea, visual changes
alternative: Artemisinin-based therapy instead of quinine where clinically appropriate

effect: Quinine potentiates warfarin, raising INR and bleeding risk.
mechanism: CYP2C9 inhibition by quinine; possible additive effect on vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.
action: Monitor INR every 2-3 days during quinine therapy.
alternative: Artemisinin-based therapy where appropriate

effect: Omeprazole (particularly at higher doses) can increase phenytoin levels, risking toxicity.
mechanism: CYP2C19 inhibition by omeprazole reduces phenytoin clearance.
action: Monitor phenytoin levels if omeprazole >20mg/day is used. Use pantoprazole as safer alternative.
alternative: Pantoprazole (weaker CYP2C19 inhibitor)

effect: Esomeprazole (like omeprazole) significantly reduces clopidogrel antiplatelet effect.
mechanism: CYP2C19 inhibition blocks clopidogrel prodrug activation.
action: Switch to pantoprazole or rabeprazole with clopidogrel.
monitoring: Cardiovascular events; platelet function if available
alternative: Pantoprazole 40mg or rabeprazole 20mg

effect: All PPIs including pantoprazole may reduce methotrexate renal excretion, raising toxicity risk (less than omeprazole but still significant with high-dose MTX).
mechanism: OAT3 transporter inhibition reduces tubular methotrexate secretion.
action: Withhold PPI around high-dose methotrexate infusions. For low-dose MTX, monitor LFTs and FBC more closely.
alternative: Famotidine (H2-blocker) as acid suppression during MTX cycles

effect: Cyclosporine increases rosuvastatin AUC by approximately 7-fold despite rosuvastatin not being CYP3A4-dependent.
mechanism: OATP1B1 inhibition by cyclosporine dramatically reduces rosuvastatin hepatic uptake and increases plasma levels.
action: Limit rosuvastatin to 5mg/day with cyclosporine. Never exceed 10mg/day.
alternative: Fluvastatin 20mg/day (relatively safer with cyclosporine)

effect: Trimethoprim inhibits renal tubular secretion of metformin, increasing its plasma levels and lactic acidosis risk.
mechanism: OCT2 transporter inhibition by trimethoprim reduces metformin renal clearance.
action: Monitor renal function. Caution in patients with any degree of renal impairment.
monitoring: Renal function (creatinine/eGFR); symptoms of lactic acidosis
alternative: Avoid co-trimoxazole where possible; use cephalosporin instead

effect: High-dose aspirin enhances sulfonylurea hypoglycaemic effect through multiple mechanisms.
mechanism: Aspirin displaces sulfonylurea from plasma proteins; also directly stimulates insulin secretion.
action: Monitor blood glucose closely if high-dose aspirin is used. Low-dose aspirin (75mg) is generally safe.
alternative: Low-dose aspirin (≤100mg) preferred; avoid anti-inflammatory doses of aspirin with sulfonylureas

effect: Rifampicin modestly reduces sitagliptin levels through P-glycoprotein induction.
mechanism: P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4 induction by rifampicin.
action: Monitor blood glucose during rifampicin co-administration. May need to increase sitagliptin dose.
alternative: Adjust dose; consider metformin as primary diabetic agent

effect: Beta-blockers mask tachycardia (a key hypoglycaemia warning symptom) in insulin-treated patients and can prolong hypoglycaemia. Non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol) are worse than cardioselective (bisoprolol).
mechanism: Beta-blockade prevents hypoglycaemia-induced tachycardia; propranolol also inhibits glycogenolysis.
action: Prefer cardioselective beta-blockers (bisoprolol, metoprolol) in insulin-treated patients. Counsel patient that palpitations as a hypoglycaemia warning may be absent; monitor glucose more frequently.
monitoring: Blood glucose; patient education about masked symptoms
alternative: Cardioselective beta-blocker (bisoprolol preferred); amlodipine or ACEi if beta-blocker avoidable

effect: Fluoroquinolones (especially gatifloxacin, moxifloxacin) cause both hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia in patients on sulfonylureas.
mechanism: Fluoroquinolones stimulate insulin secretion directly; some also inhibit CYP2C9 raising sulfonylurea levels.
action: Monitor blood glucose multiple times daily during fluoroquinolone therapy in any patient on oral antidiabetics. Ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin are safer choices.
alternative: Non-fluoroquinolone antibiotic where possible

effect: Rifampicin reduces dabigatran levels by ~66%, causing anticoagulation failure.
mechanism: P-glycoprotein induction by rifampicin reduces dabigatran absorption and increases elimination.
action: Avoid combination. Consider warfarin (better understood dosing with rifampicin) under haematology guidance.
monitoring: Thromboembolic events; dabigatran levels (ECT or dilute thrombin time)
alternative: Warfarin with very close INR monitoring; consult haematology

effect: Amiodarone increases dabigatran levels ~60% through P-glycoprotein inhibition.
mechanism: P-glycoprotein inhibition by amiodarone increases dabigatran absorption.
action: Consider dose reduction of dabigatran (150mg to 110mg twice daily) in patients on amiodarone, especially if other bleeding risk factors present.
monitoring: Bleeding signs; renal function (dabigatran primarily renally cleared)
alternative: Warfarin with INR monitoring; apixaban (less affected)

effect: Trimethoprim modestly potentiates warfarin through CYP2C9 inhibition.
mechanism: CYP2C9 inhibition by trimethoprim reduces S-warfarin clearance.
action: Monitor INR within 3-5 days of starting co-trimoxazole or trimethoprim alone.
alternative: Cephalosporin or amoxicillin where appropriate (less INR effect)

effect: Topical NSAIDs (ketorolac eye drops) may reduce the IOP-lowering effect of prostaglandin analogues.
mechanism: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, potentially counteracting prostaglandin analogue mechanism.
action: Monitor IOP when topical NSAIDs are co-prescribed with glaucoma drops.
alternative: Use topical NSAIDs only when specifically indicated; separate from glaucoma drop instillation

effect: Topical timolol (eye drops) is systemically absorbed and can cause bradycardia and AV block when combined with systemic verapamil.
mechanism: Even topical beta-blocker has significant systemic absorption — additive AV node depression with verapamil.
action: Use alternative glaucoma agent (latanoprost, brimonidine) in patients on verapamil or other rate-limiting drugs.
alternative: Latanoprost or brimonidine eye drops (no cardiac interaction)

effect: Topical timolol absorbed systemically can cause severe bradycardia with amiodarone.
mechanism: Additive AV node and sinus node depression.
action: Use alternative glaucoma drops (latanoprost, brimonidine) in patients on amiodarone.
alternative: Latanoprost 0.005% or brimonidine 0.2% eye drops

effect: Vitamin A supplements combined with isotretinoin cause additive hypervitaminosis A toxicity.
mechanism: Isotretinoin is a retinoid — additional vitamin A causes hypervitaminosis A syndrome (pseudotumour cerebri, liver toxicity).
action: Absolutely contraindicated. Patients on isotretinoin must avoid all vitamin A supplements.
alternative: No supplement needed; ensure patient counselling

effect: Acitretin (a retinoid) combined with methotrexate causes additive hepatotoxicity — both are independently hepatotoxic.
mechanism: Additive hepatotoxic mechanisms.
action: Avoid combination. If both required for severe psoriasis, consult dermatology specialist; use minimum doses and monitor LFTs monthly.
monitoring: LFTs monthly; liver biopsy may be indicated with prolonged use
alternative: Monotherapy preferred; biologics as alternative

effect: Combination causes significantly increased hepatotoxicity risk — both are independently hepatotoxic.
mechanism: Additive hepatotoxicity; leflunomide also increases methotrexate levels.
action: Avoid combination unless under specialist rheumatology supervision with monthly LFT monitoring.
alternative: Monotherapy or biologics as alternative to combination DMARD

effect: Both prolong QT interval — combination significantly increases torsades risk.
mechanism: Additive hERG potassium channel blockade.
action: Avoid combination. Monitor ECG if unavoidable.
alternative: Alternative DMARD (methotrexate, sulfasalazine) for rheumatic disease

effect: Hydroxychloroquine increases digoxin levels by approximately 70%.
mechanism: P-glycoprotein inhibition reduces digoxin renal clearance.
action: Monitor digoxin levels when hydroxychloroquine is started or stopped. Reduce digoxin dose if levels rise.
alternative: No switch needed — monitoring and dose adjustment

effect: Combination can cause increased folate deficiency and bone marrow suppression.
mechanism: Both drugs impair folate metabolism through different mechanisms.
action: Ensure adequate folic acid supplementation (5mg/week) when using combination. Monitor FBC.
alternative: Folic acid supplementation is the management — not a reason to avoid combination

effect: Carbamazepine modestly reduces levetiracetam levels — generally not clinically significant.
mechanism: Mild enzyme induction by carbamazepine slightly increases levetiracetam clearance.
action: Monitor seizure control. Dose adjustment rarely needed.
alternative: No change usually needed

effect: Phenobarbitone reduces warfarin levels significantly, increasing thromboembolism risk.
mechanism: Potent CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 induction by phenobarbitone.
action: Monitor INR closely when starting or stopping phenobarbitone. Large warfarin dose increases likely needed.
monitoring: INR every 3-5 days when initiating; weekly until stable
alternative: Levetiracetam (no enzyme induction) as antiepileptic alternative

effect: Phenobarbitone causes contraceptive failure — high-level enzyme inducer.
mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 induction massively increases ethinylestradiol and progestogen metabolism.
action: Use copper IUD or levonorgestrel IUD. If OCP must be used, use highest available dose preparation plus barrier method.
alternative: Copper IUD (most reliable with enzyme-inducing antiepileptics)

effect: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine receptors, directly opposing levodopa's therapeutic effect and worsening Parkinson's symptoms.
mechanism: Dopamine D2 receptor antagonism by metoclopramide counters levodopa-mediated dopamine replacement.
action: Never use metoclopramide as antiemetic in Parkinson's patients. Use domperidone (peripherally acting, does not cross BBB) instead.
monitoring: Parkinson's symptoms — rigidity, bradykinesia, tremor worsening
alternative: Domperidone 10mg TDS (peripheral dopamine antagonist, does not cross BBB)

effect: Haloperidol blocks dopamine receptors, directly opposing levodopa's therapeutic effect.
mechanism: Central dopamine D2 receptor antagonism by haloperidol.
action: Avoid all typical antipsychotics in Parkinson's patients. If psychosis occurs, use quetiapine (low affinity D2) or clozapine.
alternative: Quetiapine (25-50mg) or clozapine for psychosis in Parkinson's disease

effect: Trimethoprim increases amantadine levels causing toxicity — confusion, agitation, hallucinations.
mechanism: Both inhibit renal tubular secretion via OCT2; trimethoprim blocks amantadine clearance.
action: Avoid combination. Use alternative antibiotic in patients on amantadine.
alternative: Cephalosporins or beta-lactams for infections

effect: Carbapenems (meropenem, imipenem, ertapenem) rapidly reduce valproate levels by 60-100%, causing catastrophic seizure breakthrough within 24-48 hours.
mechanism: Carbapenems inhibit valproate absorption and increase its metabolism via unknown mechanisms — one of the fastest and most dramatic drug interactions.
action: Avoid all carbapenems in valproate-treated patients whenever possible. If carbapenem is necessary, switch to IV phenobarbitone or levetiracetam for seizure control during carbapenem therapy. Do NOT simply increase valproate dose — it will not compensate.
alternative: Piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, or other non-carbapenem beta-lactams where clinically feasible

effect: All NSAIDs increase lithium levels by 25-60% — risk of lithium toxicity.
mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin synthesis, reducing renal blood flow and lithium clearance.
action: Avoid all NSAIDs in lithium-treated patients. Paracetamol is the safe analgesic choice.
monitoring: Serum lithium levels within 5 days; toxicity signs (tremor, polyuria, confusion)
alternative: Paracetamol ≤2g/day for analgesia

effect: Ciprofloxacin markedly increases clozapine levels by CYP1A2 inhibition, causing severe toxicity (seizures, agranulocytosis, sedation).
mechanism: CYP1A2 inhibition dramatically raises clozapine plasma concentrations.
action: Avoid ciprofloxacin in clozapine patients. Use alternative antibiotic. If unavoidable, reduce clozapine dose by 50% and monitor levels daily.
alternative: Beta-lactam antibiotics or doxycycline

effect: Valproate can increase clozapine levels and both drugs independently lower seizure threshold.
mechanism: Possible CYP1A2 inhibition; pharmacodynamic interaction lowering seizure threshold.
action: Monitor clozapine levels. Monitor for seizures — clozapine + valproate combination used in treatment-resistant patients with seizure prophylaxis.
alternative: Lamotrigine preferred over valproate with clozapine in some guidelines

effect: Fluvoxamine dramatically increases clozapine levels 3-5 fold by potent CYP1A2 inhibition, causing severe toxicity.
mechanism: Fluvoxamine is the most potent CYP1A2 inhibitor among SSRIs.
action: Avoid combination. Use sertraline or citalopram (minimal CYP1A2 inhibition) if SSRI needed with clozapine.
alternative: Sertraline or citalopram for depression in clozapine-treated patients

effect: Fluoxetine increases haloperidol levels significantly via CYP2D6 inhibition, increasing extrapyramidal effects and QT prolongation.
mechanism: CYP2D6 inhibition by fluoxetine (strong inhibitor) raises haloperidol levels.
action: Reduce haloperidol dose when fluoxetine is added. Monitor for EPS and QT prolongation.
alternative: Sertraline (weaker CYP2D6 inhibitor) as SSRI alternative

effect: Life-threatening serotonin syndrome or opioid toxicity — case reports of death. Two distinct reactions: hyperpyrexia/serotonin toxicity OR respiratory depression.
mechanism: MAOIs prevent breakdown of serotonin; meperidine also releases serotonin and is a serotonin reuptake inhibitor.
action: Absolutely contraindicated — never combine. Use morphine (safer alternative with MAOIs after washout period).
monitoring: If combination inadvertent: temperature, BP, clonus, respiratory rate
alternative: Morphine (some evidence of safety after MAOI washout); consult specialist

effect: Serotonin syndrome — case reports of severe reactions including death from common OTC cough medicines.
mechanism: MAOIs + serotonin reuptake inhibition by dextromethorphan.
action: Absolutely contraindicated. Counsel all MAOI patients to avoid OTC cough medicines containing dextromethorphan. 14-day washout required.
alternative: Guaifenesin-based cough preparations

effect: Calcium and magnesium in antacids dramatically reduce bisphosphonate absorption (e.g., alendronate by >60%).
mechanism: Chelation of bisphosphonate by divalent cations in the gut.
action: Take bisphosphonate on empty stomach with plain water. No food, drink, or other medicines for at least 30 minutes after.
alternative: Strict administration protocol; take bisphosphonate first thing in morning with water only

effect: IV ciprofloxacin may increase risk of bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (BRONJ) in patients on IV bisphosphonates.
mechanism: Additive impairment of bone healing; fluoroquinolones may impair collagen synthesis.
action: Awareness only — not a reason to avoid ciprofloxacin when indicated. Ensure good oral hygiene and avoid dental extractions where possible.
monitoring: Oral cavity — osteonecrosis signs with prolonged IV bisphosphonate
alternative: No alternative needed — dental care precautions are primary management

effect: Trimethoprim combined with methotrexate causes severe bone marrow suppression — potentially fatal pancytopenia.
mechanism: Both drugs block dihydrofolate reductase — additive antifolate toxicity.
action: Absolutely contraindicated. Use alternative antibiotic for all infections in methotrexate-treated patients.
alternative: Cephalosporins or penicillins — avoid all antifolate antibiotics (co-trimoxazole, trimethoprim)

effect: Statins (particularly CYP3A4-dependent ones: simvastatin, atorvastatin) increase risk of colchicine myopathy when combined.
mechanism: Additive myotoxicity; some statins inhibit P-glycoprotein, increasing colchicine levels.
action: Use lowest effective colchicine dose. Prefer rosuvastatin or pravastatin (less myotoxic at therapeutic doses) in patients requiring long-term colchicine.
alternative: Rosuvastatin or pravastatin as statin; NSAIDs or prednisolone for acute gout as colchicine alternative

effect: Dofetilide has a very narrow therapeutic window — any QT-prolonging drug risks torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Additive hERG potassium channel blockade prolongs QT beyond safe limits.
action: Absolutely contraindicated to combine dofetilide with any QT-prolonging drug. Strict drug interaction screening mandatory before prescribing.
monitoring: QTc interval must be <440ms before each dose
alternative: Amiodarone or dronedarone under specialist supervision

effect: Corticosteroids reduce salicylate blood levels; if corticosteroid is stopped, aspirin toxicity can occur from rising levels.
mechanism: Corticosteroids increase renal salicylate clearance; when stopped, clearance decreases.
action: When stopping long-term corticosteroid in patient on high-dose aspirin, reduce aspirin dose to prevent rebound toxicity.
monitoring: Salicylate toxicity signs when reducing/stopping corticosteroid
alternative: Use paracetamol in preference to high-dose aspirin with corticosteroids

effect: Sucralfate reduces ciprofloxacin absorption by up to 50%.
mechanism: Sucralfate (aluminium compound) chelates ciprofloxacin in the gut.
action: Separate sucralfate and ciprofloxacin by at least 2 hours. Take ciprofloxacin first.
alternative: Separate timing — take ciprofloxacin 2 hours before sucralfate

effect: Sucralfate can reduce warfarin absorption by binding it in the gut.
mechanism: Physical binding of warfarin to sucralfate's aluminium-sucrose complex.
action: Separate sucralfate and warfarin by at least 2 hours.
monitoring: INR if sucralfate is started or stopped
alternative: PPI instead of sucralfate for GI protection in warfarin patients

effect: Cholestyramine dramatically reduces warfarin absorption and increases its elimination via bile.
mechanism: Ion exchange resin binds warfarin in the gut; also reduces enterohepatic recirculation.
action: Separate warfarin from cholestyramine by at least 4-6 hours. Monitor INR closely when starting or stopping.
alternative: Statin (without interaction) for cholesterol reduction; or ezetimibe

effect: Cholestyramine reduces levothyroxine absorption by up to 90%, causing profound hypothyroidism.
mechanism: Ion exchange resin binds levothyroxine in the gut.
action: Separate levothyroxine from cholestyramine by at least 4 hours. Take levothyroxine first.
monitoring: TSH and free T4 at 6-8 weeks after any change in cholestyramine timing
alternative: Statin or ezetimibe instead of cholestyramine where clinically appropriate

effect: Amoxicillin (like most antibiotics) can modestly potentiate warfarin through gut flora suppression.
mechanism: Gut flora suppression reduces vitamin K2 production.
action: Monitor INR 3-5 days after completing amoxicillin course in warfarin patients.
alternative: No switch needed — monitoring is the management

effect: Azithromycin may modestly increase carbamazepine levels through weak CYP3A4 inhibition.
mechanism: Weak CYP3A4 inhibition by azithromycin.
action: Generally no action required for standard 5-day azithromycin courses. Monitor for carbamazepine toxicity if prolonged azithromycin use.
alternative: No switch needed for standard short courses

effect: Additive 5-alpha reductase inhibition — combined use provides no additional benefit but increases side effects.
mechanism: Both drugs inhibit 5-alpha reductase; combination does not improve outcomes over monotherapy.
action: Avoid combining. Use monotherapy only.
alternative: Monotherapy with either agent; add alpha-blocker for BPH symptoms

effect: Standard BPH combination — modest additional BP lowering risk; well-studied and generally acceptable.
mechanism: Alpha-blockade + 5ARI — additive vasodilatory effect.
action: Standard BPH combination. Counsel patients on postural hypotension, especially in first weeks.
alternative: No change needed — monitor BP and counsel

effect: Erythromycin increases sildenafil levels by approximately 180%, increasing adverse effects (hypotension, visual disturbance, priapism).
mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition by erythromycin reduces sildenafil clearance.
action: Reduce sildenafil starting dose to 25mg. Avoid multiple doses during erythromycin course.
monitoring: Blood pressure, visual disturbance, prolonged erection
alternative: Use non-macrolide antibiotic; or reduce sildenafil dose

effect: Clarithromycin significantly increases tadalafil exposure, raising adverse effect risk.
mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition by clarithromycin.
action: Reduce tadalafil dose; avoid >10mg dose during clarithromycin therapy.
alternative: Use azithromycin or doxycycline instead of clarithromycin

effect: Loss of glycaemic control and hyperglycaemia.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, accelerating sulfonylurea metabolism and lowering glibenclamide exposure.
action: Avoid when possible. Monitor capillary blood glucose closely and expect sulfonylurea dose escalation or temporary insulin requirement during rifampicin therapy.
monitoring: Fasting and post-prandial glucose, symptoms of hyperglycaemia
alternative: Consider insulin while on rifampicin if control worsens.

effect: Reduced gliclazide effect with worsening blood sugar control.
mechanism: Rifampicin enzyme induction increases gliclazide clearance.
action: Monitor glucose closely; dose adjustment or temporary insulin may be needed during rifampicin therapy.
monitoring: Blood glucose, HbA1c if prolonged course
alternative: Insulin or non-induced antihyperglycaemic strategy during rifampicin treatment.

effect: Reduced sulfonylurea exposure causing hyperglycaemia.
mechanism: Potent induction of CYP2C9 lowers glimepiride levels.
action: Monitor glucose and consider up-titration or temporary insulin while rifampicin is used.
alternative: Insulin if control becomes unstable.

effect: Reduced carbamazepine concentration and breakthrough seizures or neuralgia recurrence.
mechanism: Rifampicin strongly induces CYP3A4, increasing carbamazepine metabolism.
action: Avoid if possible. If used together, monitor symptoms and carbamazepine concentration; dose increase may be needed.
monitoring: Carbamazepine level, seizure control, dizziness/ataxia if dose adjusted
alternative: Choose a non-enzyme-inducing antibiotic if feasible.

effect: Reduced steroid exposure and treatment failure.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4, increasing dexamethasone clearance.
action: Avoid when possible or increase steroid dose based on clinical response.
monitoring: Clinical response, inflammatory symptoms, blood glucose if dose increased
alternative: Use non-inducing antimicrobial regimen where possible.

effect: Additive QT prolongation with risk of torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Both agents can prolong ventricular repolarization through hERG/IKr effects.
action: Avoid routine co-prescribing in high-risk patients; correct potassium and magnesium and use ECG monitoring if unavoidable.
alternative: Metoclopramide or non-QT-prolonging antibiotic depending on indication.

effect: QT prolongation and torsades risk.
mechanism: Additive pharmacodynamic QT prolongation.
action: Avoid when feasible, especially in elderly patients, heart disease, or low K/Mg.
alternative: Use a non-QT-prolonging antiemetic or antibiotic if possible.

effect: Potentially serious QT prolongation.
mechanism: Both prolong QT; fluconazole may additionally raise exposure of some co-medications.
action: Avoid in high-risk patients; ECG monitoring if combined.
alternative: Alternative antiemetic or topical antifungal when clinically appropriate.

effect: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes risk.
mechanism: Additive QT-prolonging effect; both are higher risk in electrolyte disturbance or structural heart disease.
action: Avoid combination, especially at higher domperidone doses.
alternative: Use non-QT-prolonging antiemetic where possible.

effect: QT prolongation and arrhythmia risk.
mechanism: Additive QT effect; fluoxetine may also increase domperidone exposure through CYP interactions in some patients.
action: Avoid if possible; choose alternative antiemetic.
alternative: Metoclopramide if appropriate and not otherwise contraindicated.

effect: Marked rise in quetiapine exposure causing oversedation, hypotension, and QT risk.
mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, the main pathway for quetiapine metabolism.
action: Avoid. If unavoidable, consider large quetiapine dose reduction with close monitoring.
monitoring: Sedation, BP, ECG if high risk
alternative: Use non-macrolide antibiotic if possible.

effect: QT prolongation and arrhythmia risk.
mechanism: Additive QT-prolonging effect.
action: Avoid in patients with other QT risks; monitor ECG if unavoidable.
alternative: Alternative antibiotic where possible.

effect: Reduced antihypertensive effect and acute kidney injury risk.
mechanism: NSAID-mediated prostaglandin inhibition reduces renal perfusion; ARB lowers efferent arteriolar tone.
action: Avoid prolonged co-use, especially in CKD, dehydration, or elderly patients.
alternative: Paracetamol for pain if suitable.

effect: Reduced BP control and kidney injury risk.
mechanism: Combined afferent/efferent renal hemodynamic effects reduce GFR; NSAIDs also blunt antihypertensive response.
action: Avoid chronic co-use; check renal function after initiation if necessary.
alternative: Paracetamol when appropriate.

effect: Increased risk of acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia.
mechanism: NSAID renal vasoconstriction combines with potassium-sparing diuresis.
action: Avoid if possible, especially in CKD or elderly patients.
alternative: Paracetamol for analgesia if suitable.

effect: Hyperkalaemia and renal impairment.
mechanism: NSAID-induced fall in renal perfusion plus potassium-sparing effect of spironolactone.
action: Avoid prolonged combination; monitor closely if short course unavoidable.
alternative: Paracetamol when appropriate.

effect: Clinically significant hyperkalaemia.
mechanism: ARB lowers aldosterone-mediated potassium excretion while KCl increases potassium load.
action: Avoid routine supplementation unless clearly indicated; recheck potassium soon after starting.
monitoring: Serum potassium, ECG if symptomatic/high risk
alternative: Dietary review or lower-dose replacement with close monitoring.

effect: Hyperkalaemia and arrhythmia risk.
mechanism: ACE inhibitor reduces aldosterone; supplemental potassium increases total body potassium burden.
action: Avoid routine KCl with ACE inhibitor unless carefully monitored.
monitoring: Serum potassium, creatinine, ECG if high risk
alternative: Use only if clearly indicated with lab follow-up.

effect: Large reduction in levofloxacin absorption and possible antibiotic failure.
mechanism: Chelation in the GI tract forms poorly absorbed complexes.
action: Separate doses by at least 2 hours before or 4-6 hours after calcium.
alternative: Use IV antibiotic or alter administration timing.

effect: Marked fall in ciprofloxacin absorption leading to treatment failure.
mechanism: Chelation in the GI tract.
action: Do not give together; separate by at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after antacid.
alternative: Avoid antacid during short antibiotic course if possible.

effect: Reduced doxycycline absorption and possible treatment failure.
mechanism: Chelation in the gut lowers tetracycline bioavailability.
action: Separate by at least 2-3 hours.
alternative: Different antacid timing or different antibiotic class.

effect: Lithium accumulation and neurotoxicity.
mechanism: Metronidazole can reduce lithium renal clearance, increasing serum lithium concentrations.
action: Avoid if possible. If unavoidable, monitor lithium level and watch for tremor, confusion, ataxia.
monitoring: Lithium level, renal function, neurological status
alternative: Use different antibiotic when feasible.

effect: Possible rise in phenytoin level and toxicity or altered metronidazole exposure.
mechanism: CYP2C9/CYP2C19 interaction may raise phenytoin concentration while phenytoin can induce metronidazole metabolism.
action: Use with caution; monitor for nystagmus, ataxia, slurred speech and seizure control.
alternative: Alternative antibiotic if high-risk patient.

effect: Raised phenytoin concentration with toxicity risk.
mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP2C19, reducing phenytoin clearance.
action: Avoid or monitor phenytoin concentration and neurological adverse effects.
alternative: Topical or non-azole antifungal if appropriate.

effect: Raised carbamazepine level with dizziness, diplopia, ataxia, and nausea.
mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4-mediated carbamazepine metabolism.
action: Avoid or reduce carbamazepine dose and monitor level/symptoms.
alternative: Alternative antifungal when feasible.

effect: Possible INR rise and bleeding risk in susceptible patients.
mechanism: Likely reduced vitamin K-producing gut flora with occasional pharmacokinetic contribution.
action: Check INR within several days of starting or stopping azithromycin in warfarin users.
alternative: Alternative antibiotic not necessary in all patients; monitoring is usually sufficient.
cyp_pathway: Minimal CYP effect; gut flora effect

effect: Increased drowsiness and impaired psychomotor performance.
mechanism: Additive CNS depressant effects.
action: Advise patient to avoid alcohol until individual sensitivity is known.
alternative: Non-sedating measures; counsel on night dosing if appropriate.

effect: Additive sedation and reduced alertness.
mechanism: CNS depressant pharmacodynamic interaction.
action: Avoid alcohol when first starting or when dose increased.
alternative: Counsel on nighttime dosing if needed.

effect: Higher frequency of aminopenicillin rash.
mechanism: Long-recognized association, exact mechanism uncertain.
action: Counsel and monitor for rash; consider alternative antibiotic if history of drug rash.
alternative: Alternative antibiotic where appropriate.

effect: Possible reduction in clopidogrel activation; generally less concern than omeprazole but still worth consistency review.
mechanism: Pantoprazole has weaker CYP2C19 inhibition than omeprazole, so interaction risk is lower but not zero in some datasets.
action: Usually preferred over omeprazole when a PPI is needed with clopidogrel. Flag for clinician review rather than absolute avoidance.
alternative: Pantoprazole is often the alternative to omeprazole; keep for review not hard-stop.

effect: Reduced iron absorption and poorer hematinic response.
mechanism: Calcium interferes with iron absorption in the gut.
action: Separate administration by at least 2 hours.
alternative: Different timing of doses.

effect: Marked fall in quetiapine exposure with relapse of psychosis, insomnia, or agitation.
mechanism: Rifampicin strongly induces CYP3A4, the main metabolic pathway for quetiapine.
action: Avoid if possible. If co-use is unavoidable, monitor clinical response closely and expect substantial antipsychotic dose adjustment or alternative selection.
monitoring: Psychiatric symptoms, sedation, orthostatic symptoms after any dose change
alternative: Consider an antipsychotic less affected by CYP3A4 induction when feasible.

effect: Reduced haloperidol concentration with loss of symptom control.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces hepatic metabolism of haloperidol, lowering serum exposure.
action: Prefer alternative antimicrobial therapy when feasible or monitor closely for psychotic symptom recurrence; dose increase may be needed during rifampicin use.
monitoring: Psychiatric symptoms, EPS after dose changes
alternative: Use non-enzyme-inducing therapy if clinically suitable.

effect: Loss of anxiolytic and sedative effect.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4, accelerating alprazolam clearance.
action: Avoid combination or anticipate reduced benzodiazepine effect. Reassess anxiety control rather than escalating indefinitely.
monitoring: Anxiety symptoms, sedation failure, withdrawal symptoms
alternative: Consider lorazepam if clinically appropriate because it is less CYP3A4-dependent.

effect: Reduced diazepam exposure and shorter sedative effect.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 and related oxidative metabolism of diazepam.
action: Use cautiously; monitor response and prefer a less affected benzodiazepine if ongoing TB treatment is needed.
monitoring: Anxiety, muscle spasm control, oversedation after dose changes
alternative: Lorazepam may be easier to manage during rifampicin therapy.

effect: Reduced analgesic effect with inadequate pain control.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 and UGT pathways, lowering tramadol and active metabolite exposure.
action: Avoid where possible. Use alternative analgesia and monitor for pain escalation.
monitoring: Pain score, sedation, withdrawal if chronic tramadol user
alternative: Use non-opioid analgesia or supervised alternative opioid strategy if needed.

effect: Substantial reduction in tadalafil effect and erectile-dysfunction treatment failure.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4, greatly increasing tadalafil clearance.
action: Avoid co-prescribing when possible. Counsel that PDE5 inhibitor response may be markedly reduced.
monitoring: Clinical response, hypotension if dose adjusted
alternative: Delay PDE5 therapy until rifampicin ends when feasible.

effect: Marked loss of sildenafil efficacy.
mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 induction lowers sildenafil exposure.
action: Avoid or warn the patient that effect may be poor. Do not simply escalate to unsafe doses without specialist review.
monitoring: Clinical response, dizziness or hypotension if dose changes are attempted
alternative: Postpone sildenafil use until rifampicin therapy is complete when possible.

effect: INR elevation and bleeding risk.
mechanism: Isoniazid inhibits warfarin metabolism, especially via CYP2C9 and CYP2C19-related pathways, increasing anticoagulant effect.
action: Check INR early after starting or stopping isoniazid and adjust warfarin dose promptly.
alternative: Closer anticoagulation follow-up during anti-TB treatment.

effect: Higher risk of hepatotoxicity, especially in malnutrition or alcohol use.
mechanism: Isoniazid can alter acetaminophen metabolism and both drugs contribute to hepatic injury risk.
action: Use the lowest effective paracetamol dose and avoid prolonged high-dose use. Counsel about liver toxicity symptoms.
monitoring: LFTs if prolonged use, nausea, jaundice, RUQ pain
alternative: Short-course low-dose paracetamol with monitoring rather than repeated maximum dosing.

effect: Serotonin toxicity and seizure risk.
mechanism: Additive serotonergic activity; tramadol also lowers seizure threshold.
action: Avoid when possible. Prefer non-serotonergic analgesia and educate about agitation, sweating, tremor, diarrhea, or confusion.
monitoring: Mental status, tremor, clonus, temperature, seizure activity
alternative: Paracetamol or other non-serotonergic pain strategy if appropriate.

effect: Additive QT prolongation with torsades risk.
mechanism: Both medicines delay cardiac repolarization and increase arrhythmia risk, especially with hypokalaemia or high doses.
action: Avoid if possible. Correct potassium and magnesium and choose a different antiemetic or antipsychotic when feasible.
alternative: Use lower-risk antiemetic options when clinically acceptable.

effect: Increased QT prolongation risk, especially in dehydration or electrolyte loss.
mechanism: Both agents can prolong QT; risk rises with higher doses and low potassium.
action: Avoid routine combination if alternatives exist. If unavoidable, correct electrolytes and consider ECG monitoring.
alternative: Use a lower-risk antiemetic or review antipsychotic choice.

effect: High-risk QT prolongation and torsades potential.
mechanism: Additive effect on ventricular repolarization.
action: Avoid if possible. ECG monitoring is advisable if the combination cannot be avoided.
alternative: Choose an antiemetic with less QT liability if suitable.

effect: QT prolongation with torsades risk.
mechanism: Azithromycin and escitalopram both prolong QT; risk increases with female sex, older age, and electrolyte disturbance.
action: Prefer a non-QT-prolonging antibiotic when possible. If used together, correct electrolytes and consider ECG review.
alternative: Use an antibiotic with lower QT burden if clinically appropriate.

effect: Possible additive QT prolongation in susceptible patients.
mechanism: Both can influence cardiac repolarization, though sertraline risk is usually lower than citalopram/escitalopram.
action: Use carefully in high-risk patients and correct electrolytes. Avoid stacking other QT-prolonging medicines.
alternative: Consider non-macrolide antibiotic if overall QT burden is high.

effect: Excess sedation, confusion, and psychomotor impairment.
mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, markedly increasing alprazolam exposure.
action: Avoid or hold alprazolam during the macrolide course if feasible. Warn against driving and alcohol.
alternative: Use lorazepam temporarily if a benzodiazepine is essential.

effect: Enhanced sedation and impaired coordination.
mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition can raise diazepam exposure, though effect is usually less dramatic than with alprazolam or midazolam.
action: Use lower doses and monitor sedation if the combination cannot be avoided.
alternative: Prefer lorazepam if benzodiazepine cover is essential.

effect: Colchicine toxicity with GI symptoms, myopathy, and marrow suppression risk.
mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4 and can reduce colchicine clearance, especially with renal dysfunction.
action: Avoid if possible or reduce colchicine dose substantially with careful monitoring.
monitoring: Diarrhea, muscle pain, CK, CBC, renal function
alternative: Select a non-interacting antifungal when feasible.

effect: Potentially severe colchicine accumulation leading to life-threatening toxicity.
mechanism: Voriconazole is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor and may markedly increase colchicine exposure.
action: Avoid combination. Choose another antifungal or withhold colchicine with specialist advice.
monitoring: CBC, CK, renal function, GI toxicity, neuromuscular symptoms
alternative: Use a lower-interaction antifungal or pause colchicine if clinically acceptable.

effect: Higher apixaban exposure and bleeding risk.
mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4 and may also affect P-gp, increasing apixaban levels.
action: Use cautiously or avoid in high-bleeding-risk patients. Watch closely for bruising or bleeding.
alternative: Use a non-azole antifungal or specialist-guided anticoagulation plan.

effect: Raised dabigatran levels with bleeding risk.
mechanism: Verapamil inhibits P-glycoprotein, increasing dabigatran absorption and exposure.
action: Use dose reduction or avoid depending on renal function and formulation timing. Specialist review is preferred.
alternative: Consider alternative rate-control or anticoagulant strategy if risk is high.

effect: Lithium accumulation with tremor, confusion, and toxicity.
mechanism: Reduced renal lithium clearance due to effects on sodium handling and renal perfusion.
action: Avoid where possible. If used, check lithium level after initiation and after dose changes.
monitoring: Lithium level, creatinine, tremor, confusion, GI upset
alternative: Use a different antihypertensive where practical.

effect: Lithium level rise and toxicity risk.
mechanism: Diuretic-related sodium shifts can reduce renal lithium clearance.
action: Avoid if possible. If unavoidable, monitor lithium concentration and renal function closely.
monitoring: Lithium level, creatinine, tremor, ataxia, confusion
alternative: Review need for spironolactone or choose a different mood-stabilizer/antihypertensive combination.

effect: Reduced levothyroxine absorption with rising TSH and worsening hypothyroid symptoms.
mechanism: Higher gastric pH reduces dissolution and absorption of levothyroxine.
action: Separate if possible and recheck thyroid status after persistent PPI use.
alternative: Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach consistently and review need for chronic PPI.

effect: Marked reduction in levothyroxine absorption and treatment failure.
mechanism: Sucralfate binds levothyroxine in the gut.
action: Separate by several hours and monitor TSH after starting or stopping sucralfate.
alternative: Use acid-suppression strategies that do not bind levothyroxine if appropriate.

effect: Postural dizziness and symptomatic hypotension.
mechanism: Additive vasodilation from PDE5 inhibition and alpha-1 blockade.
action: Start at the lowest doses and counsel about standing up slowly. Avoid taking first doses together.
alternative: Space initiation and titration cautiously under supervision.

effect: Higher risk of acute kidney injury, particularly in dehydration or existing renal impairment.
mechanism: Additive renal tubular stress and reduced renal reserve.
action: Avoid repeated NSAID use in patients taking tenofovir. Use safer analgesia and check renal function if exposure occurs.
alternative: Prefer paracetamol when clinically suitable.

effect: Increased upper-GI bleeding and ulcer risk.
mechanism: Additive gastric mucosal injury from corticosteroid plus NSAID therapy.
action: Avoid routine co-use if possible or add gastroprotection and warn about black stool, abdominal pain, and vomiting blood.
monitoring: GI bleeding symptoms, hemoglobin if prolonged
alternative: Use the lowest effective NSAID duration or choose non-NSAID analgesia.

effect: Hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury risk; diuretic effect may also be blunted.
mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin-mediated perfusion while spironolactone retains potassium.
action: Avoid prolonged co-use. Check potassium and renal function when combination cannot be avoided.
alternative: Prefer paracetamol or short, carefully monitored NSAID exposure only.

effect: Reduced diuretic response and worsening edema or renal function.
mechanism: NSAID-mediated prostaglandin inhibition reduces renal blood flow and attenuates loop diuretic effect.
action: Avoid repeated NSAID use in volume-sensitive patients. Reassess weight gain, swelling, and renal function.
monitoring: Weight, edema, blood pressure, creatinine, urine output
alternative: Paracetamol is often safer for analgesia in diuretic-dependent patients.

effect: Reduced diuretic effectiveness with fluid retention and renal stress.
mechanism: NSAID effect on renal prostaglandins reduces loop-diuretic natriuresis.
action: Avoid prolonged co-prescribing, especially in heart failure. Monitor edema and renal function.
alternative: Use non-NSAID analgesia when feasible.

effect: Near-complete loss of bisphosphonate absorption if taken together.
mechanism: Calcium binds the bisphosphonate in the gut and prevents absorption.
action: Do not take together. Bisphosphonate should be taken first on an empty stomach with plain water; calcium later in the day.
alternative: Dose separation is usually the best solution.

effect: More dystonia, akathisia, or parkinsonian symptoms plus sedation.
mechanism: Additive dopamine blockade and CNS adverse effects.
action: Avoid routine use together when alternatives exist. Use the shortest antiemetic course and watch for movement disorders.
alternative: Choose a lower-EPS-risk antiemetic if suitable.

effect: Possible increase in digoxin exposure with nausea, bradycardia, or toxicity.
mechanism: Macrolide-related changes in gut flora and P-gp handling can raise digoxin levels, though azithromycin is usually less problematic than clarithromycin.
action: Use cautiously, especially in older adults or renal impairment. Watch for digoxin toxicity symptoms.
monitoring: Heart rate, digoxin level if available, nausea, visual symptoms
alternative: Consider non-macrolide antibiotic if overall risk is high.

effect: Higher risk of severe allopurinol hypersensitivity and poorer uric-acid control.
mechanism: Thiazides can reduce urate excretion and may increase hypersensitivity risk in susceptible patients.
action: Use carefully, especially in renal impairment. Review need for thiazide and counsel to report rash immediately.
alternative: Use another antihypertensive if gout or allopurinol hypersensitivity risk is high.

effect: Marked nephrotoxicity risk.
mechanism: Additive renal tubular toxicity from two nephrotoxic agents.
action: Avoid if possible. If life-saving co-use is unavoidable, monitor renal function very closely and optimize hydration.
alternative: Use a less nephrotoxic antimicrobial combination if possible.

effect: Severe nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity risk.
mechanism: Additive renal and inner-ear toxicity.
action: Avoid combination unless absolutely necessary and under close inpatient monitoring.
monitoring: Creatinine, urine output, electrolytes, hearing/balance symptoms
alternative: Seek infectious-disease input for safer combinations if available.

effect: Significantly increased bleeding risk.
mechanism: Anticoagulation plus NSAID-related platelet dysfunction and GI mucosal injury.
action: Avoid where possible. Use paracetamol for pain unless there is a clear reason for NSAID use and specialist oversight.
alternative: Paracetamol is generally safer for simple analgesia.

effect: Higher bleeding risk, especially GI bleeding.
mechanism: Additive anticoagulant effect and NSAID-related mucosal injury.
action: Avoid routine co-use. Use non-NSAID analgesia whenever possible.
alternative: Prefer paracetamol for pain unless clinician directs otherwise.

effect: Potentially dangerous hyperkalaemia, especially in older adults or renal impairment.
mechanism: Both reduce renal potassium excretion.
action: Avoid combination if possible. If co-use is unavoidable, check potassium very early and consider an alternative antibiotic.
alternative: Choose a non-trimethoprim antibiotic when feasible.

effect: Hyperkalaemia and renal dysfunction risk.
mechanism: ACE inhibition plus trimethoprim-related potassium retention.
action: Avoid or monitor potassium and renal function closely, especially in older adults or CKD.
alternative: Use an alternative antibiotic when practical.

effect: Hyperkalaemia and kidney injury risk.
mechanism: ARB effect on aldosterone plus trimethoprim-related potassium retention.
action: Avoid when possible. If necessary, arrange early laboratory monitoring.
alternative: Select another antibiotic if possible.

effect: QT prolongation and increased haloperidol exposure with arrhythmia/EPS risk.
mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP pathways and both drugs can prolong QT.
action: Avoid if feasible. If unavoidable, review dose and ECG, and correct electrolytes.
alternative: Use a different antifungal or antipsychotic when possible.

effect: Higher quetiapine exposure with sedation, hypotension, and QT concerns.
mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and also carries QT risk.
action: Avoid if possible. If used, reduce quetiapine dose and monitor closely.
alternative: Choose a non-macrolide antibiotic if clinically suitable.

effect: Very high torsades risk from marked QT prolongation.
mechanism: Both agents strongly prolong ventricular repolarization; clarithromycin may also inhibit metabolism of co-administered QT-active drugs.
action: Do not co-prescribe. Select a different antibiotic urgently.
alternative: Use a non-macrolide antibiotic when possible.

effect: More sedation and psychomotor impairment.
mechanism: Fluoxetine inhibits CYP pathways that contribute to alprazolam clearance and adds CNS depressant burden.
action: Use cautiously and warn about drowsiness; titrate slowly if combination is necessary.
alternative: Review benzodiazepine need and consider non-sedating anxiety strategies.

effect: More akathisia, dystonia, or serotonin-like adverse effects.
mechanism: Additive CNS effects; fluoxetine also inhibits CYP2D6, which may increase metoclopramide exposure.
action: Avoid repeated use together when possible. Use the shortest metoclopramide course and monitor closely.
alternative: Use a lower-risk antiemetic if appropriate.

effect: Raised methadone level with oversedation, respiratory depression, and QT risk.
mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits methadone metabolism and both drugs may prolong QT.
action: Use cautiously with dose review; monitor sedation and ECG in higher-risk patients.
alternative: Use another antifungal when practical or lower methadone dose under supervision.

effect: Potentially reduced antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel plus increased bleeding from SSRI-related platelet dysfunction.
mechanism: Fluoxetine inhibits CYP2C19, which is needed to activate clopidogrel, while SSRIs can impair platelet serotonin function.
action: Review the need for fluoxetine in patients dependent on clopidogrel efficacy and consider a lower-interaction antidepressant if appropriate.
alternative: Sertraline may be easier to combine in some patients, with clinician review.

effect: Bradycardia, hypotension, and possible heart block.
mechanism: Additive AV-node suppression; diltiazem may also reduce metoprolol clearance.
action: Use cautiously and only with a clear indication. Monitor pulse and blood pressure closely after initiation or dose changes.
monitoring: Heart rate, blood pressure, dizziness, ECG if symptomatic
alternative: Avoid double rate-slowing combinations unless a cardiology plan exists.

effect: Substantial bleeding risk including GI bleeding.
mechanism: Anticoagulation plus NSAID-induced platelet dysfunction and mucosal damage.
action: Avoid where possible. Prefer non-NSAID analgesia and review all other antithrombotics.
alternative: Paracetamol is generally safer for uncomplicated pain.

effect: Possible additive QT prolongation in susceptible patients; serotonin-related symptoms are less likely but possible.
mechanism: Combined QT burden, especially with dehydration or electrolyte loss.
action: Usually avoid stacking multiple QT-prolonging medicines in high-risk patients. Correct potassium and magnesium if needed.
alternative: Choose a lower-QT antiemetic if the total burden is high.

effect: Raised theophylline concentration with nausea, tremor, tachycardia, or seizures.
mechanism: Macrolide inhibition of theophylline metabolism increases serum levels.
action: Avoid if possible or monitor theophylline level and symptoms closely.
monitoring: Theophylline level if available, heart rate, tremor, nausea
alternative: Use a non-macrolide antibiotic when feasible.

effect: Additive glucose-lowering effect can cause hypoglycaemia, especially when meals are delayed or insulin dose is unchanged.
mechanism: Acarbose blunts carbohydrate absorption while insulin lowers serum glucose independently.
action: Use together with glucose monitoring. Consider lowering insulin dose if recurrent hypoglycaemia occurs.
alternative: No direct substitute needed — titrate insulin

effect: Alcohol can convert acitretin into etretinate, prolonging fetal risk and systemic exposure for months to years.
mechanism: Transesterification in the presence of ethanol increases formation of long-persisting etretinate.
action: Avoid alcohol completely during acitretin therapy and for the recommended post-treatment period.
monitoring: Alcohol use history, pregnancy prevention adherence

effect: Calcium markedly reduces alendronate absorption and may cause treatment failure.
mechanism: Chelation/complex formation in the gut prevents oral bisphosphonate absorption.
action: Take alendronate on an empty stomach with plain water; delay calcium by at least 30 minutes, preferably longer.

effect: Iron reduces alendronate absorption and may blunt efficacy.
mechanism: Oral iron complexes with bisphosphonates and interferes with GI uptake.
action: Separate doses by several hours; alendronate should be taken first on an empty stomach.

effect: Combination may increase risk of hypersensitivity reactions and rarely blood dyscrasias, especially in renal impairment.
mechanism: Mechanism is uncertain; risk appears higher with concomitant ACE inhibitor exposure and reduced renal clearance.
action: Use cautiously, especially in CKD. Counsel patient to report rash, fever, sore throat, or mucosal lesions promptly.
monitoring: Rash, CBC if clinically indicated, renal function

effect: Warfarin effect may increase, raising bleeding risk.
mechanism: Allopurinol can reduce metabolism of warfarin in some patients.
action: Monitor INR more closely after starting or increasing allopurinol.

effect: Aminophylline/theophylline exposure can rise, causing nausea, tremor, tachycardia, or seizures.
mechanism: Macrolides inhibit theophylline clearance, increasing serum concentrations.
action: Avoid if possible or reduce aminophylline dose and monitor levels/clinical toxicity closely.

effect: Theophylline exposure may increase, especially with higher allopurinol doses.
mechanism: Allopurinol can inhibit theophylline metabolism in some patients.
action: Monitor for theophylline toxicity and consider level checks if symptoms appear.

effect: Theophylline clearance may decrease, causing concentration-related adverse effects.
mechanism: Ethinyl estradiol-containing contraceptives can reduce hepatic metabolism of theophylline.
action: Monitor for aminophylline/theophylline toxicity and adjust dose if needed.

effect: Tamoxifen can reduce anastrozole exposure and compromise aromatase-inhibitor effect.
mechanism: Tamoxifen lowers anastrozole plasma concentrations; the combination is generally avoided in routine therapy.
action: Do not combine routinely unless a specialist protocol explicitly requires it.

effect: Acetazolamide toxicity can increase, particularly in older adults or renal impairment.
mechanism: Salicylates may reduce protein binding and renal clearance of acetazolamide while contributing to acid-base disturbance.
action: Avoid high-dose aspirin. If unavoidable, monitor closely for tinnitus, lethargy, acidosis, or rapid breathing.
monitoring: Mental status, acid-base status, renal function

effect: Combination can increase myelosuppression and leukopenia.
mechanism: Additive folate and bone-marrow toxicity increases risk of cytopenia.
action: Avoid when possible. If co-use is necessary, check CBC promptly and counsel on infection warning signs.

effect: Additive QT prolongation may trigger torsades de pointes.
mechanism: Both medicines prolong ventricular repolarization and increase QT interval.
action: Avoid if possible. If unavoidable, monitor ECG and correct potassium/magnesium.

effect: Bedaquiline exposure may increase and QT/hepatotoxicity risk may rise.
mechanism: Ritonavir inhibits CYP3A-mediated metabolism of bedaquiline.
action: Use only with specialist oversight. Monitor ECG and liver function.

effect: Tetracycline absorption falls substantially, risking treatment failure.
mechanism: Calcium chelates tetracyclines in the gut and prevents absorption.
action: Separate calcium-containing products and tetracycline by several hours.

effect: Mutual enzyme induction can lower concentrations and destabilize seizure control; phenobarbital also increases sedative burden.
mechanism: Both induce hepatic enzymes and alter each other's metabolism.
action: Monitor seizure control and, where available, drug levels after dose changes.

effect: Cefalexin exposure increases and adverse effects may become more likely.
mechanism: Probenecid inhibits renal tubular secretion of cefalexin.
action: Usually not dangerous but consider lower cephalosporin exposure expectations and monitor GI intolerance/rash.

effect: Markedly increased GI, renal, and bleeding toxicity from dual NSAID therapy.
mechanism: Additive COX inhibition increases ulceration, bleeding, and renal vasoconstriction.
action: Avoid using two systemic NSAIDs together.
alternative: Use single-agent analgesia

effect: Methotrexate exposure may rise, increasing marrow and renal toxicity risk.
mechanism: NSAIDs can reduce renal elimination of methotrexate.
action: Use caution, especially with higher methotrexate doses or renal impairment. Monitor CBC/RFT.

effect: Cephalosporin exposure may rise modestly and adverse effects may be more likely.
mechanism: Probenecid reduces renal tubular secretion of cephalosporins.
action: Usually manageable; monitor for intolerance and use with awareness of higher antibiotic exposure.

effect: Severe additive nephrotoxicity can occur.
mechanism: Both drugs can impair renal perfusion/tubular function.
action: Avoid if possible. If unavoidable, monitor tacrolimus trough and renal function very closely.
monitoring: Serum creatinine, tacrolimus trough, urine output

effect: Tacrolimus exposure can rise sharply, causing nephrotoxicity, tremor, and hypertension.
mechanism: Diltiazem inhibits CYP3A4/P-gp, which normally clear tacrolimus.
action: Use only with deliberate tacrolimus dose reduction and trough monitoring.

effect: INR may increase and serious bleeding can occur.
mechanism: Bicalutamide can potentiate coumarin anticoagulation, likely via protein-binding/metabolic effects.
action: Check INR frequently after starting or stopping bicalutamide.

effect: Severe additive nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity can occur.
mechanism: Both are nephrotoxic/ototoxic agents; combined exposure increases renal and auditory injury risk.
action: Avoid if possible. If unavoidable, monitor renal function and hearing closely.

effect: Albendazole concentrations may fall, reducing antiparasitic efficacy.
mechanism: Phenytoin induces hepatic enzymes that increase albendazole metabolism.
action: Consider clinical follow-up and specialist advice if prolonged therapy is intended.

effect: Albendazole concentrations may fall, reducing efficacy.
mechanism: Carbamazepine induces hepatic metabolism of albendazole.
action: Monitor clinical response if co-use is necessary.

effect: Albendazole exposure may decrease, potentially reducing efficacy.
mechanism: Antiretroviral enzyme effects can alter albendazole metabolism.
action: Use clinical follow-up if prolonged co-use is required.

effect: Amantadine effect may be reduced and extrapyramidal balance may worsen.
mechanism: Metoclopramide opposes dopaminergic activity while amantadine supports it.
action: Avoid when feasible in Parkinsonian patients; monitor symptom control.

effect: Spironolactone diuretic response may be reduced and renal risk may rise.
mechanism: NSAID-mediated prostaglandin inhibition can blunt renal/hemodynamic effects of spironolactone.
action: Use the lowest effective aspirin dose and monitor BP, edema, and renal function.

effect: Additive immunosuppression and myelosuppression may increase infection/cytopenia risk.
mechanism: Both suppress immune cell function and marrow reserve.
action: Use with specialist monitoring; check CBC and watch for infection.

effect: Steroid exposure can fall, reducing clinical effect.
mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A-mediated corticosteroid metabolism.
action: Monitor response; higher corticosteroid doses may be needed while rifampicin is used.

effect: Bleeding risk increases because carboplatin can suppress platelets and aspirin impairs platelet function.
mechanism: Additive effects on haemostasis increase bleeding tendency.
action: Avoid routine aspirin unless specifically indicated; monitor platelets and bleeding.

effect: Nephrotoxicity risk may increase, especially in vulnerable patients.
mechanism: Both can stress renal function; loop diuretics may worsen renal injury risk with some beta-lactams/aminoglycosides.
action: Monitor renal function and hydration in high-risk patients.

effect: Rash and hypersensitivity risk may increase.
mechanism: Allopurinol increases the likelihood of aminopenicillin-associated exanthems.
action: Use with caution and counsel patient to report rash promptly.

effect: Bacteriostatic tetracyclines may theoretically reduce bactericidal penicillin effect in some settings.
mechanism: Pharmacodynamic antagonism between bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics is possible but often not clinically important.
action: Usually avoid unnecessary overlap unless specifically intended by the prescriber.

effect: Additive nephrotoxicity can be severe.
mechanism: Both drugs can independently cause renal injury.
action: Avoid if possible or monitor renal function intensively.
